title: Variational Iterative Rotation Algorithm: Combinatorial Optimization with Classical Kicked Tops
summary: We investigate a classical formulation of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), realized as a Hamiltonian dynamical system of classical kicked tops, which we call the Variational Iterative Rotation Algorithm (VIRAL). The variational parameters are the transverse and longitudinal rotation angles at each of the p layers of the circuit. We find that VIRAL outperforms QAOA on the canonical Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin-glass benchmark at all circuit depths, with the energy density converging to the ground state value linearly in 1/p. For large circuit depths, the optimized dynamics follows a Floquet protocol in which a pitchfork bifurcation destabilizes the equatorial fixed point and drives the spins toward polar Ising configurations. Our results demonstrate that the effectiveness of QAOA-like protocols derives primarily from their underlying iterative rotation structure, and that a classical implementation of it outperforms its quantum counterpart. We further elucidate its efficiency by reducing the many-body classical evolution to an effective Landau-Lifshitz dynamics for a single spin in a stochastic magnetic field. In this picture, the covariance matrix of the effective field reveals a nearly rank-one structure in which a single mode dominates the stochastic dynamics. In contrast, quantum fluctuations make the noise covariance of the effective quantum model of higher rank, hampering the control of the system. We propose nanometer-scale magnetic tunnel junctions as a natural physical platform for implementing VIRAL, where spin rotations can be realized using magnetic fields and spin torques.

AI.tldr: A classical formulation of QAOA called VIRAL (Variational Iterative Rotation Algorithm) outperforms quantum QAOA on spin-glass problems, converging linearly with circuit depth via a Floquet protocol with pitchfork bifurcation.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the effectiveness of QAOA-like protocols stems primarily from their iterative rotation structure rather than quantum effects, and to develop a classical analog that could outperform quantum implementations.
AI.method: Developed VIRAL as a Hamiltonian dynamical system of classical kicked tops with variational transverse/longitudinal rotation angles at each circuit layer. Analyzed performance on Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin-glass benchmark and reduced many-body dynamics to effective Landau-Lifshitz single-spin model in stochastic field.
AI.result: VIRAL outperforms QAOA at all circuit depths, with energy density converging linearly in 1/p to ground state. Large-depth dynamics follow Floquet protocol with pitchfork bifurcation driving spins toward polar Ising configurations. Classical noise covariance has nearly rank-one structure (single dominant mode), while quantum fluctuations create higher-rank noise hampering control.
AI.conclusion: QAOA's effectiveness derives primarily from iterative rotation structure, not quantum effects. Classical VIRAL implementation outperforms quantum QAOA. Magnetic tunnel junctions proposed as physical platform for implementing VIRAL using magnetic fields and spin torques.

title: Isolated extended states and anomalous critical behavior in the generalized SSH model
summary: We investigate the localization properties of a generalized SSH model. Numerical and analytical results indicate the emergence of extended states protected by unbounded hopping in this model. Moreover, this protection effect is disrupted by the appearance of generalized incommensurate zeros, causing the extended phase in the system to transition into a multifractal phase. However, at the boundaries of the phase region, we still observe the existence of extended states. These extended states coincide with multifractality-enriched mobility edges, separating the multifractal phase from the localized phase. Further analysis reveals that this extended states originates from the band edge states of SSH model. In addition, these isolated extended states also influence eigenstates with nearby energies, giving rise to an anomalous extended-to-multifractal critical transition. These findings not only enrich the behavioral repertoire of eigenstates at critical points, but also offer new insights for further understanding Anderson localization and the induction of multifractal phases.

AI.tldr: Extended states emerge in a generalized SSH model due to unbounded hopping, but are disrupted by generalized incommensurate zeros, leading to multifractal phases with mobility edges separating multifractal and localized phases.
AI.motivation: To investigate localization properties and eigenstate behaviors in a generalized SSH model, particularly examining how unbounded hopping protects extended states and how generalized incommensurate zeros disrupt this protection, leading to multifractal phases.
AI.method: Combined numerical and analytical approaches to study the generalized SSH model, analyzing the effects of unbounded hopping and generalized incommensurate zeros on eigenstate localization and phase transitions.
AI.result: Extended states emerge protected by unbounded hopping but are disrupted by generalized incommensurate zeros, causing extended-to-multifractal transitions. At phase boundaries, extended states persist and coincide with multifractality-enriched mobility edges separating multifractal and localized phases. These extended states originate from SSH model band edge states and influence nearby eigenstates.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals rich eigenstate behaviors at critical points, including anomalous extended-to-multifractal transitions and multifractality-enriched mobility edges, providing new insights into Anderson localization and multifractal phase induction mechanisms.

title: Crossovers from nonlinear wave-packet acceleration to wave-mixing and self-trapping in the Hatano-Nelson model
summary: We demonstrate that wave amplification enables even weak nonlinearities to reshape linear wave-packet transport in nonreciprocal systems. We study the dynamics of bulk Gaussian wave packets in the Hatano--Nelson model with onsite cubic nonlinearity. We show that the interplay between nonlinearity and amplification generates growing frequency shifts that drive the wave packet through three successive dynamical regimes: an early nonlinear-skin regime with coherent propagation, an intermediate wave-mixing regime driven by mode resonances, and a self-trapping regime in which part of the packet localizes while the remainder ballistically spreads along the system favored direction. The crossover time scales are set by the width and average spacing of the eigen-frequency spectrum. Crucially, within the nonlinear-skin regime, we derive analytical predictions for the wave-packet dynamics and show that nonlinearity couples amplification, dispersion, and nonreciprocity, thereby modifying the magnitude of the wave-packet acceleration and introducing an explicit time dependence into its evolution. Focusing nonlinearities suppress the acceleration and cause it to decrease in time, whereas defocusing nonlinearities enhance it and cause it to increase. We further show that nonlinear interactions typically break down the wave packet before the non-Hermitian jump can occur. Our results provide a route toward accurate control of waves in nonreciprocal metamaterials.

AI.tldr: Nonlinearity reshapes wave transport in nonreciprocal systems through amplification-driven frequency shifts, creating three dynamical regimes: nonlinear-skin, wave-mixing, and self-trapping.
AI.motivation: To understand how weak nonlinearities can significantly alter linear wave-packet transport in nonreciprocal systems through wave amplification effects.
AI.method: Study bulk Gaussian wave packets in the Hatano-Nelson model with onsite cubic nonlinearity, analyzing interplay between nonlinearity and amplification through analytical predictions and dynamical regime analysis.
AI.result: Three successive dynamical regimes emerge: early nonlinear-skin regime with coherent propagation, intermediate wave-mixing regime driven by mode resonances, and self-trapping regime with partial localization and ballistic spreading. Nonlinearity couples amplification, dispersion, and nonreciprocity, modifying wave-packet acceleration with time-dependent evolution.
AI.conclusion: Wave amplification enables weak nonlinearities to dramatically reshape nonreciprocal wave transport, with nonlinear interactions typically preventing non-Hermitian jumps and providing routes for precise wave control in nonreciprocal metamaterials.

title: Robust Correlation-Induced Localization Under Time-Reversal Symmetry Breaking
summary: We study Anderson localization in a one-dimensional disordered system with long-range correlated hopping decaying as $1/r^{a}$ with complex hopping amplitudes that break time-reversal symmetry in a tunable fashion by varying their argument. We find analytically a corelation-induced algebraic localization that is robust to a finite strength of the time-reversal-symmetry-breaking parameter, beyond which all states delocalize. This establishes a localization--delocalization transition driven by the interplay between long-ranged correlated hopping and time-reversal symmetry breaking. In addition to obtaining the static localization phase diagram, we also investigate the dynamical phase diagram through the lens of wavepacket spreading. We find that the growth in time of the mean-squared displacement of a wavepacket, which is subdiffusive for the time-reversal symmetric case, becomes diffusive for any finite value of the time-reversal-symmetry-breaking parameter.

AI.tldr: Anderson localization in 1D disordered system with long-range correlated hopping (decaying as 1/r^a) and complex hopping amplitudes that break time-reversal symmetry. Algebraic localization persists up to finite symmetry-breaking strength, beyond which all states delocalize, creating a localization-delocalization transition.
AI.motivation: To understand the interplay between long-range correlated hopping and time-reversal symmetry breaking in disordered quantum systems, particularly how these factors influence Anderson localization and delocalization transitions.
AI.method: Analytical study of a one-dimensional disordered system with long-range correlated hopping decaying as 1/r^a with complex hopping amplitudes. The time-reversal symmetry breaking is tunable by varying the argument of the hopping amplitudes. Both static localization properties and dynamical behavior through wavepacket spreading are investigated.
AI.result: 1) Correlation-induced algebraic localization that remains robust up to a finite strength of time-reversal symmetry breaking parameter. 2) Beyond a critical value, all states delocalize, establishing a localization-delocalization transition. 3) Dynamically, wavepacket spreading shows subdiffusive growth in mean-squared displacement for time-reversal symmetric case, but becomes diffusive for any finite value of symmetry-breaking parameter.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals a rich phase diagram where the interplay between long-range correlated hopping and time-reversal symmetry breaking drives a localization-delocalization transition. The transition is characterized by both static localization properties and dynamical behavior, with symmetry breaking fundamentally altering transport from subdiffusive to diffusive.

title: Hybrid Classical--Quantum Optimization of Wireless Routing Using QAOA and Quantum Walks
summary: Routing in wireless communication networks is shaped by mobility, interference, congestion, and competing service requirements, making route selection a high-dimensional constrained optimization problem rather than a simple shortest-path task. This paper investigates the use of hybrid classical--quantum methods for wireless routing, focusing on the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and quantum walks as candidate mechanisms for exploring complex routing spaces. The paper examines how wireless routing can be expressed as a constrained graph optimization problem in which routing objectives, flow constraints, connectivity requirements, and interference effects are mapped into quantum-compatible Hamiltonian representations. It then discusses how these approaches can be integrated into a hybrid architecture in which classical systems perform network monitoring, graph construction, pre-processing, and deployment, while quantum subroutines are used for selected optimization components. The analysis shows that the potential value of quantum routing lies primarily in the treatment of difficult combinatorial subproblems rather than end-to-end replacement of classical routing frameworks. The paper also highlights practical limitations arising from state preparation, constraint encoding, oracle construction, hardware noise, limited qubit resources, and hybrid execution overhead. It is argued that any meaningful near-term advantage will depend on careful problem decomposition, compact encoding, and tight classical--quantum integration.

AI.tldr: Hybrid classical-quantum methods (QAOA and quantum walks) are investigated for wireless routing optimization, showing potential for solving combinatorial subproblems within classical frameworks rather than replacing them entirely.
AI.motivation: Wireless routing involves high-dimensional constrained optimization due to mobility, interference, congestion, and service requirements, making it more complex than simple shortest-path problems. Classical approaches struggle with these combinatorial complexities, motivating exploration of quantum methods.
AI.method: Map wireless routing to constrained graph optimization problems with routing objectives, flow constraints, connectivity requirements, and interference effects encoded into quantum-compatible Hamiltonian representations. Use hybrid architecture where classical systems handle network monitoring, graph construction, pre-processing, and deployment, while quantum subroutines (QAOA and quantum walks) optimize selected components.
AI.result: Quantum routing shows potential primarily for difficult combinatorial subproblems rather than end-to-end replacement of classical routing frameworks. Practical limitations include state preparation, constraint encoding, oracle construction, hardware noise, limited qubit resources, and hybrid execution overhead.
AI.conclusion: Near-term quantum advantage for wireless routing depends on careful problem decomposition, compact encoding, and tight classical-quantum integration. Quantum methods should be integrated as specialized optimization components within existing classical routing frameworks rather than as complete replacements.

title: Exhaustive Optimisation of Automorphism Groups for Stabiliser Codes
summary: An important measure of utility for a quantum code is the identification of which logical operations can be implemented fault-tolerantly on its codespace. We introduce a framework which leverages the automorphism groups of associated classical codes, the choice of logical basis and exploitation of code equivalence to construct all distinct implementable realisations of each valid logical operation for a given $[[n,k,d]]$ code. We establish conjugacy classes and group transversals (unrelated to transversality) as key explanatory concepts. We subsequently motivate and calculate two figures-of-merit that can be optimised with this framework. Our results yield a table of optimal logical operations and their corresponding physical circuits for all small stabiliser codes with $n \leq 7$ and $k \leq 2$, drawn from quantum databases. This exhaustive table of results provides the optimal physical implementations of logical operations which may be advantageous for both magic state cultivation and experimental purposes.

AI.tldr: Framework for constructing all distinct fault-tolerant logical operations on quantum codes using classical code automorphism groups, logical basis choice, and code equivalence, with optimal implementations for small stabilizer codes.
AI.motivation: To systematically identify and implement all fault-tolerant logical operations on quantum codes, which is crucial for quantum error correction and practical quantum computing applications like magic state cultivation.
AI.method: Leverages automorphism groups of associated classical codes, logical basis selection, and code equivalence to construct all distinct implementable realizations of valid logical operations. Uses conjugacy classes and group transversals as key explanatory concepts.
AI.result: Developed framework yields optimal logical operations and corresponding physical circuits for all small stabilizer codes with n ≤ 7 and k ≤ 2, drawn from quantum databases, providing exhaustive table of optimal implementations.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables systematic construction of fault-tolerant logical operations with optimization metrics, providing optimal physical implementations beneficial for both magic state cultivation and experimental quantum computing.

title: Bootstrapping Symmetries in Quantum Many-Body Systems from the Cross Spectral Form Factor
summary: Symmetries play a central role in quantum many-body physics, yet uncovering them systematically remains challenging. We introduce a bootstrap framework designed to reconstruct the representation theory of hidden finite group symmetries of quantum many-body lattice Hamiltonians, using only a known symmetry subgroup $N$ and spectral correlations between its symmetry sectors. We introduce a novel variant of the spectral form factor, the cross spectral form factor (xSFF), which we compute via exact diagonalization to seed the bootstrap algorithm. By applying the constraints derived from these data alongside the algebraic conditions of the fusion rules, our bootstrap procedure sharply restricts the set of candidate groups $G$. Remarkably, without any prior assumptions regarding the full symmetry group $G$, our method can systematically recover its representation-theoretic data, including the number and dimensions of the irreducible representations, their branching rules with respect to $N$, the fusion algebra, and the full character table. This framework applies equally well to chaotic and integrable many-body systems and accommodates both unitary and anti-unitary symmetries. Through various examples, we demonstrate that the underlying group $G$ can be uniquely identified. In particular, our bootstrap independently recovers the $\mathbb{Z}_4$ symmetry at the self-dual point of the three-state quantum torus chain, detects signatures of projective representations in the effective Hamiltonian of the driven Bose-Hubbard model, and rediscovers the $η$-pairing $\mathrm{SO}(4)$ symmetry of the one-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model. Our framework thus establishes a practical route to identify symmetries directly from dynamical spectral observables.

AI.tldr: A bootstrap framework reconstructs hidden finite group symmetries of quantum many-body Hamiltonians using spectral correlations and known subgroup symmetries.
AI.motivation: Symmetries are fundamental in quantum many-body physics but are difficult to uncover systematically. Existing methods often require prior knowledge of the full symmetry group, creating a need for data-driven approaches that can discover hidden symmetries directly from spectral data.
AI.method: Introduces a bootstrap framework using cross spectral form factor (xSFF) computed via exact diagonalization. Combines spectral correlation data from known subgroup N with algebraic constraints from fusion rules to restrict candidate groups G. The method systematically recovers representation-theoretic data without prior assumptions about G.
AI.result: The framework successfully identifies hidden symmetries in various systems: recovers Z4 symmetry at the self-dual point of the three-state quantum torus chain, detects projective representations in the driven Bose-Hubbard model, and rediscovers the η-pairing SO(4) symmetry of the 1D Fermi-Hubbard model. The method uniquely identifies underlying groups and works for both chaotic and integrable systems with unitary and anti-unitary symmetries.
AI.conclusion: The bootstrap framework establishes a practical, data-driven route to identify symmetries directly from dynamical spectral observables, enabling systematic discovery of hidden finite group symmetries in quantum many-body systems without requiring prior knowledge of the full symmetry group.

title: Numerically Optimizing Shortcuts to Adiabaticity: A Hybrid Control Strategy
summary: Achieving fast, excitation-free quantum control is a vital challenge in modern quantum technologies. In many cases, shortcuts to adiabaticity enable fast adiabatic-like protocols, yet determining control parameters that satisfy practical constraints is often challenging in complex systems. Here, we combine an analytical shortcut to adiabaticity approach with several numerical optimization methods to boost the performance of the protocol. As a proof-of-principle for this hybrid approach, we study a particularly intricate control problem, the separation of two trapped ions. We show that this analytical-numerical approach, along with the physical insight gained through the variety of suboptimal solutions, leads to the exploration of new solutions in a complex landscape that yield improvements of up to 3 orders of magnitude. Moreover, this improvement comes with no additional cost from an experimental point of view.

AI.tldr: Hybrid analytical-numerical approach combines shortcuts to adiabaticity with optimization methods to achieve fast, excitation-free quantum control for trapped ion separation with 3 orders of magnitude improvement.
AI.motivation: Need for fast, excitation-free quantum control in complex systems where determining practical control parameters is challenging; existing shortcuts to adiabaticity approaches often struggle with practical constraints.
AI.method: Combines analytical shortcut to adiabaticity approach with numerical optimization methods (hybrid analytical-numerical approach); uses trapped ion separation as proof-of-principle test case.
AI.result: Achieves improvements up to 3 orders of magnitude in protocol performance; explores new solutions in complex landscape; gains physical insight from suboptimal solutions; no additional experimental cost.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid analytical-numerical approach effectively boosts quantum control performance, enabling practical solutions for complex control problems like trapped ion separation with significant speed improvements.

title: Constructing Fermionic Dynamics with Closed Moment Hierarchies
summary: We construct a broad class of completely positive maps and Go\-rini--Kossakowski--Sudarshan-Lindblad generators for fermionic systems induced by linear transformations of system and environment modes. For these maps, we derive explicit Heisenberg-picture formulas for arbitrary normally ordered monomials in terms of minors of the underlying mode-transformation matrices and environment correlation tensors. We show that for even environment states the linear span of monomials up to any fixed order is invariant, which yields closed equations for low-order moments and makes their computation efficient. We also discuss the relation of this construction to second quantization of non-Hermitian one-particle contractions and extend the formalism to completely positive maps arising from post-selection.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a mathematical framework for constructing completely positive maps and GKSL generators for fermionic systems using linear transformations of system and environment modes, with explicit formulas for normally ordered monomials and efficient computation of low-order moments.
AI.motivation: To develop a systematic construction of completely positive maps and GKSL generators for fermionic open quantum systems that allows for explicit computation of correlation functions and efficient treatment of low-order moments.
AI.method: Constructs completely positive maps and GKSL generators induced by linear transformations of system and environment modes. Derives explicit Heisenberg-picture formulas for arbitrary normally ordered monomials using minors of mode-transformation matrices and environment correlation tensors. Shows invariance of linear span of monomials up to fixed order for even environment states, enabling closed equations for low-order moments.
AI.result: Obtains explicit formulas for correlation functions in terms of minors and environment correlation tensors. Demonstrates efficient computation of low-order moments through closed equations. Extends formalism to completely positive maps from post-selection and relates construction to second quantization of non-Hermitian one-particle contractions.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a powerful tool for analyzing fermionic open quantum systems with explicit computational formulas and efficient treatment of correlation functions, particularly useful for systems with even environment states and low-order moment calculations.

title: Programmable recirculating bricks mesh architecture for quantum photonics
summary: General-purpose programmable photonic processors offer a flexible foundation for integrating various functionalities within a single chip. A two-dimensional hexagonal waveguide mesh of Mach Zehnder interferometers has been shown to have great potential in the field of microwave photonics. Additionally, they are a promising platform for the creation of unitary linear transformations, which are key elements in photonic neural networks, In this article, we expand the portfolio of available applications for recirculating bricks mesh architecture to quantum technologies. We will show that a single programmable optical system is capable of performing various functions depending on the requirements. In particular, we will focus in this work on boson sampling, a task that best demonstrates quantum advantage, as well as on tasks that enable the determination of photon indistinguishability, which plays a key role in photonic quantum technologies. We will also show that, in addition to spatial modes, the same optical system can be equally well-suited for work on temporal modes through the implementation of an appropriate number of loops.

AI.tldr: A programmable photonic processor based on hexagonal waveguide mesh can be adapted for quantum applications including boson sampling and photon indistinguishability measurements, with capability to work in both spatial and temporal modes.
AI.motivation: To expand the application portfolio of recirculating bricks mesh architecture from classical microwave photonics and photonic neural networks to quantum technologies, demonstrating that a single programmable optical system can perform multiple quantum functions.
AI.method: Utilizes a two-dimensional hexagonal waveguide mesh of Mach Zehnder interferometers as a programmable photonic processor, adapting it for quantum applications by implementing appropriate configurations and loops for temporal mode operation.
AI.result: The system is shown capable of performing boson sampling (demonstrating quantum advantage) and tasks for determining photon indistinguishability, with equal suitability for both spatial and temporal modes through loop implementation.
AI.conclusion: A single programmable photonic processor based on hexagonal waveguide mesh can serve multiple quantum technology applications, bridging classical photonic processing with quantum information processing capabilities.

title: Resource Estimation via Efficient Compilation of Key Quantum Primitives
summary: Resource estimation is a significant challenge in evaluating fault tolerant quantum computers. Existing approaches often rely on either fixed architectural assumptions or coarse analytical models that fail to capture the interaction between hardware constraints and circuit compilation. This challenge is particularly acute for neutral atom quantum computers, where architectural features such as atom movement, measurement zones, and multi-species arrays introduce a broad design space for implementing fault tolerant computation. Addressing the need for a tighter feedback loop between hardware design and practical application development, we present a compilation-driven framework for quantum resource estimation that translates arbitrary quantum circuits into logical primitive operations with known physical resource costs. This framework allows for easily configurable hardware assumptions that enable rapid comparison of different architectural design choices. We apply our approach to two early fault tolerant quantum simulation and optimization workloads, assuming the use of the surface code, revealing several architectural trends. While the production of magic states continues to be the dominant source of overhead for these benchmarks, access to movement can save time on cultivation and important transversal gates. As problem size grows, routing and qubit movement become dominant bottlenecks, highlighting the need for movement-aware compiler optimizations and frugal routing strategies. Finally, our results suggest that neutral atom architectures combining dual-species arrays with controlled qubit movement offer a promising path toward near-term advantage on fault tolerant devices.

AI.tldr: A compilation-driven framework for quantum resource estimation that enables rapid comparison of architectural design choices for neutral atom quantum computers, revealing that magic state production dominates overhead but movement capabilities can save time, with routing becoming a bottleneck as problem size grows.
AI.motivation: Existing resource estimation approaches for fault tolerant quantum computers either rely on fixed architectural assumptions or coarse analytical models that fail to capture hardware-circuit interactions. This is particularly problematic for neutral atom quantum computers where features like atom movement, measurement zones, and multi-species arrays create a broad design space that needs tighter integration between hardware design and application development.
AI.method: The authors present a compilation-driven framework that translates arbitrary quantum circuits into logical primitive operations with known physical resource costs. The framework allows for easily configurable hardware assumptions, enabling rapid comparison of different architectural design choices. They apply this approach to two early fault tolerant quantum simulation and optimization workloads, assuming the use of the surface code.
AI.result: Magic state production remains the dominant source of overhead for the benchmarks studied. However, access to movement capabilities can save time on cultivation and important transversal gates. As problem size grows, routing and qubit movement become dominant bottlenecks. The results highlight the need for movement-aware compiler optimizations and frugal routing strategies.
AI.conclusion: Neutral atom architectures combining dual-species arrays with controlled qubit movement offer a promising path toward near-term advantage on fault tolerant devices. The compilation-driven framework provides valuable insights for architectural design by enabling rapid comparison of different hardware configurations and their impact on practical quantum workloads.

title: Quantum polymorphism characterisation of commutativity gadgets in all quantum models
summary:
Commutativity gadgets provide a technique for lifting classical reductions between constraint satisfaction problems to quantum-sound reductions between the corresponding nonlocal games. We develop a general framework for commutativity gadgets in the setting of quantum homomorphisms between finite relational structures. Building on the notion of quantum homomorphism spaces, we introduce a uniform notion of commutativity gadget capturing the finite-dimensional quantum, quantum approximate, and commuting-operator models. In the robust setting, we use the weighted-algebra formalism for approximate quantum homomorphisms to capture corresponding notions of robust commutativity gadgets.
  Our main results characterize both non-robust and robust commutativity gadgets purely in terms of quantum polymorphism spaces: in any model, existence of a commutativity gadget is equivalent to the collapse of the corresponding quantum polymorphisms to classical ones at arity $|A|^2$, and robust gadgets are characterized by stable commutativity of the appropriate weighted polymorphism algebra. We use this characterisation to show relations between the classes of commutativity gadget, notably that existence of a robust commutativity gadget is equivalent to the existence of a corresponding non-robust one.
  Finally, we prove that quantum polymorphisms of complete graphs $K_n$ have a very special structure, wherein the noncommutative behaviour only comes from the quantum permutation group $S_n^+$. Combining this with techniques from combinatorial group theory, we construct separations between commutativity-gadget classes: we exhibit a relational structure admitting a finite-dimensional commutativity gadget but no quantum approximate gadget, and, conditional on the existence of a non-hyperlinear group, a structure admitting a quantum approximate commutativity gadget but no commuting-operator gadget.

AI.tldr: Commutativity gadgets lift classical CSP reductions to quantum nonlocal games; framework developed for quantum homomorphisms; gadgets characterized via quantum polymorphism collapse; robust/non-robust equivalence; separations between gadget classes constructed.
AI.motivation: To develop a general framework for commutativity gadgets in quantum homomorphisms between relational structures, enabling lifting of classical constraint satisfaction reductions to quantum-sound reductions between nonlocal games across different quantum models.
AI.method: Develop uniform notion of commutativity gadget using quantum homomorphism spaces and weighted-algebra formalism; characterize gadgets via quantum polymorphism spaces collapse; use combinatorial group theory and quantum permutation groups to construct separations between gadget classes.
AI.result: Characterization theorems: commutativity gadget existence equivalent to quantum polymorphisms collapsing to classical at arity |A|²; robust gadgets characterized by stable commutativity of weighted polymorphism algebra; robust/non-robust equivalence; separations: structure with finite-dimensional gadget but no quantum approximate gadget, and conditional structure with quantum approximate gadget but no commuting-operator gadget.
AI.conclusion: Commutativity gadgets provide systematic connection between classical CSP reductions and quantum nonlocal games; characterization via polymorphism collapse offers powerful theoretical framework; separations reveal hierarchy among quantum models for commutativity gadgets.

title: Distributed Variational Quantum Linear Solver
summary: This paper develops a distributed variational quantum algorithm for solving large-scale linear equations. For a linear system of the form $Ax=b$, the large square matrix $A$ is partitioned into smaller square block submatrices, each of which is known only to a single noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) computer. Each NISQ computer communicates with certain other quantum computers in the same row and column of the block partition, where the communication patterns are described by the row- and column-neighbor graphs, both of which are connected. The proposed algorithm integrates a variant of the variational quantum linear solver at each computer with distributed classical optimization techniques. The derivation of the quantum cost function provides insight into the design of the distributed algorithm. Numerical quantum simulations demonstrate that the proposed distributed quantum algorithm can solve linear systems whose size scales with the number of computers and is therefore not limited by the capacity of a single quantum computer.

AI.tldr: A distributed variational quantum algorithm for solving large-scale linear equations by partitioning the matrix across multiple NISQ computers with coordinated optimization.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limited capacity of single NISQ computers by enabling solution of large-scale linear systems through distributed quantum computing across multiple quantum processors.
AI.method: Partitions large matrix A into smaller square block submatrices distributed across multiple NISQ computers, each communicating with row- and column-neighbors via connected graphs. Integrates variational quantum linear solver variants at each node with distributed classical optimization techniques.
AI.result: Numerical quantum simulations demonstrate the algorithm can solve linear systems whose size scales with the number of computers, overcoming single quantum computer capacity limitations.
AI.conclusion: The distributed variational quantum algorithm enables solving large-scale linear systems by leveraging multiple NISQ computers, with communication patterns defined by row- and column-neighbor graphs, providing a scalable approach beyond single quantum processor limitations.

title: Classical shadows with arbitrary group representations
summary: Classical shadows (CS) has recently emerged as an important framework to efficiently predict properties of an unknown quantum state. A common strategy in CS protocols is to parametrize the basis in which one measures the state by a random group action; many examples of this have been proposed and studied on a case-by-case basis. In this work, we present a unified theory that allows us to simultaneously understand CS protocols based on sampling from general group representations, extending previous approaches that worked in simplified (multiplicity-free) settings. We identify a class of measurement bases which we call "centralizing bases" that allows us to analytically characterize and invert the measurement channel, minimizing classical post-processing costs. We complement this analysis by deriving general bounds on the sample-complexity necessary to obtain estimates of a given precision. Beyond its unification of previous CS protocols, our method allows us to readily generate new protocols based on other groups, or different representations of previously considered ones. For example, we characterize novel shadow protocols based on sampling from the spin and tensor representations of $\textsf{SU}(2)$, symmetric and orthogonal groups, and the exceptional Lie group $G_2$.

AI.tldr: A unified theory for classical shadows protocols based on general group representations, extending beyond multiplicity-free settings, with analytical characterization of measurement channels and sample complexity bounds.
AI.motivation: Classical shadows framework has emerged as important for efficiently predicting quantum state properties, but existing protocols use random group actions on a case-by-case basis without unified theory for general group representations.
AI.method: Develop unified theory for CS protocols based on sampling from general group representations, identify "centralizing bases" that allow analytical characterization and inversion of measurement channel, derive sample complexity bounds, and apply to various groups.
AI.result: Theory extends previous approaches beyond multiplicity-free settings, enables analytical channel inversion minimizing classical post-processing, provides general sample complexity bounds, and generates new protocols for various groups including SU(2), symmetric/orthogonal groups, and G₂.
AI.conclusion: Provides unified framework for classical shadows protocols based on general group representations, enabling systematic protocol design, analytical characterization, and extension to new groups beyond previously considered cases.

title: Twisted Fiber Bundle Codes over Group Algebras
summary: We introduce a twisted fiber-bundle construction of quantum CSS codes over group algebras \(R=\mathbb F_2[G]\), where each base generator carries a generator-dependent \(R\)-linear fiber twist satisfying a flatness condition. This construction extends the untwisted lifted product code, recovered when all twists are identities. We show that invertible twists (satisfying a flatness condition) give a complex chain-isomorphic to the untwisted one, so the resulting binary CSS codes have the same blocklength \(n\) and encoded dimension \(k\). In contrast, singular chain-compatible twists can lower boundary ranks and increase the number of logical qubits. Examples over \(R=\mathbb F_2[D_3]\) show that the twisted fiber bundle code can outperform the corresponding untwisted lifted-product code in \(k\) while keeping the same \(n\) and, in our examples, the same minimum distance \(d\).

AI.tldr: Twisted fiber-bundle construction of quantum CSS codes over group algebras that extends untwisted lifted product codes, where singular twists can increase logical qubits while maintaining blocklength and potentially distance.
AI.motivation: To develop a more general construction of quantum CSS codes that extends the untwisted lifted product framework, allowing for generator-dependent twists that can potentially improve code parameters (specifically increasing logical qubits k while keeping blocklength n constant).
AI.method: Introduces a twisted fiber-bundle construction over group algebras R = 𝔽₂[G], where each base generator carries a generator-dependent R-linear fiber twist satisfying a flatness condition. The construction generalizes untwisted lifted product codes (which are recovered when all twists are identities). Analyzes invertible vs. singular twists and their effects on chain complexes.
AI.result: Invertible twists satisfying flatness yield chain-isomorphic complexes to untwisted case, preserving n and k. Singular chain-compatible twists can lower boundary ranks and increase logical qubits k. Examples over R = 𝔽₂[D₃] demonstrate twisted codes can outperform corresponding untwisted lifted-product codes in k while maintaining same n and, in examples, same minimum distance d.
AI.conclusion: The twisted fiber-bundle construction provides a flexible framework for designing quantum CSS codes that can achieve better parameters than untwisted lifted product codes, particularly by increasing logical qubit count without increasing blocklength, while potentially preserving distance.

title: Practical Tomography of Multi-Time Processes
comment: 10 pages including supplementary. Version 1. Comments are welcome
summary: Characterising multi-time quantum processes is essential for analysing temporally correlated noise and for designing effective control and mitigation strategies. A complete operational description through multi-time process tomography requires an informationally complete set of probes, which necessarily includes non-deterministic intermediate operations. On present-day quantum devices, such operations are commonly implemented using mid-circuit measurements and reset, which are technologically limited and can introduce noise and overhead in terms of ancilla requirement. In this work, we study the minimal ancillary dimension required for complete characterisation of multi-time processes. We show that sequential interactions with a single qubit ancilla can generate an informationally complete family of correlated probes for processes of arbitrary length, without requiring mid-circuit measurements or reset. Our result provides a resource-efficient route for complete multi-time process tomography and establishes that one qubit of coherent ancillary memory suffices for full reconstruction of arbitrary multi-time dynamics.

AI.tldr: One qubit of coherent ancillary memory suffices for complete multi-time quantum process tomography without mid-circuit measurements or reset.
AI.motivation: Current multi-time process tomography requires non-deterministic intermediate operations implemented via mid-circuit measurements and reset, which introduce noise, overhead, and technological limitations. There's a need for resource-efficient characterization of temporally correlated quantum noise.
AI.method: Study minimal ancillary dimension required for complete multi-time process characterization. Show that sequential interactions with a single qubit ancilla can generate an informationally complete family of correlated probes for arbitrary-length processes, eliminating need for mid-circuit measurements or reset.
AI.result: Demonstrate that one qubit of coherent ancillary memory is sufficient for full reconstruction of arbitrary multi-time quantum dynamics. This provides a resource-efficient route for complete multi-time process tomography.
AI.conclusion: Complete characterization of multi-time quantum processes can be achieved with minimal resources—just one qubit of coherent ancillary memory—without the drawbacks of mid-circuit measurements and reset operations, enabling more efficient quantum noise analysis and control strategy design.

title: The Quantum Walk Characteristic Polynomial Distinguishes All Strongly Regular Graphs of Prime Orde
summary:
Let $G$ be a strongly regular graph of prime order $p$ with connection degree $k \geq 6$. We prove that the \emph{quantum walk characteristic polynomial} $χ_q(G,λ) \coloneqq \det(λI - U_G)$, where $U_G$ is the coined quantum walk operator on $G$, completely determines $G$ up to isomorphism within the class of strongly regular graphs of the same order.
  The proof proceeds in three steps. First, we show that $U_G$ block-diagonalizes under the discrete Fourier transform over $\Z_p$, yielding $p$ blocks $U_G^{(j)}$ of size $k \times k$. Second, we prove an explicit formula \[
  χ_q\!\bigl(U_G^{(j)}, λ\bigr) =
  (λ-1)^{(k-2)/2}(λ+1)^{(k-2)/2}
  \!\left(λ^2 - \tfrac{2\widehat{A}_G(j)}{k}\,λ+ 1\right), \] from which the Fourier coefficient $\widehat{A}_G(j)$ is recovered as the unique real part of an eigenvalue of $U_G^{(j)}$ distinct from $\pm 1$. Third, the inverse discrete Fourier transform recovers the connection set $S$ of $G$, and Turner's theorem (1967) identifies $G$ up to isomorphism. As a consequence, graph isomorphism is decidable in polynomial time within this class using the quantum walk spectrum, without resorting to the general quasi-polynomial algorithm of Babai (2016).

AI.tldr: Quantum walk characteristic polynomial uniquely determines strongly regular graphs of prime order p with k≥6 up to isomorphism, enabling polynomial-time graph isomorphism decision.
AI.motivation: To establish a polynomial-time algorithm for graph isomorphism within the class of strongly regular graphs of prime order, avoiding the need for Babai's quasi-polynomial general algorithm.
AI.method: Three-step approach: 1) Block-diagonalize quantum walk operator via discrete Fourier transform over ℤₚ, 2) Derive explicit formula for characteristic polynomial of each block to recover Fourier coefficients, 3) Use inverse Fourier transform to reconstruct connection set and apply Turner's theorem for isomorphism identification.
AI.result: The quantum walk characteristic polynomial χ_q(G,λ) completely determines strongly regular graphs of prime order p with connection degree k≥6 up to isomorphism within the class, enabling polynomial-time graph isomorphism decision.
AI.conclusion: Quantum walks provide an efficient tool for graph isomorphism on strongly regular graphs of prime order, offering polynomial-time complexity compared to the general quasi-polynomial algorithm.

title: Codimension-controlled universality of quantum Fisher information singularities at topological band-touching defects
summary: Topological phase transitions in generic multiband systems are mediated by band-touching defects whose codimension -- the number of momentum directions along which the gap closes linearly -- varies across universality classes. Although singular behavior of fidelity susceptibilities and quantum Fisher information (QFI) has been computed for specific models, no unifying principle connecting these results has been identified: it has remained unclear whether the controlling variable is spatial dimensionality, band structure, or an intrinsic geometric property of the defect. We resolve this question by showing that the singular contribution to the QFI with respect to the tuning parameter $m$ obeys a universal power-law scaling $\sim |m|^{p-2}$ for $p \neq 2$, with a logarithmic divergence $\sim \ln(1/|m|)$ at the marginal codimension $p = 2$, where $p$ denotes the codimension of the band-touching defect. This exponent is independent of spatial dimensionality, anisotropies, ultraviolet regularization, and additional gapped bands, and is protected by renormalization-group arguments at the linearized fixed point. The result unifies previously isolated observations for SSH chains ($p=1$), Chern insulators ($p=2$), and Weyl semimetals ($p=3$) as instances of a single codimension-dependent universality class, and reveals that only defects with $p \leq 2$ generate divergent information-geometric responses. This establishes a direct and previously missing link between topological classification in momentum space and quantum distinguishability in parameter space, with implications for metrological sensitivity near topological transitions and for the experimental detection of topological criticality via quantum geometric observables.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a universal scaling law for quantum Fisher information (QFI) near topological phase transitions, showing it scales as ∼|m|^{p-2} (logarithmic at p=2) where p is the codimension of band-touching defects, unifying various topological systems under a single codimension-dependent universality class.
AI.motivation: To identify the unifying principle connecting singular behavior of fidelity susceptibilities and quantum Fisher information across different topological phase transitions, resolving whether the controlling variable is spatial dimensionality, band structure, or an intrinsic geometric property of the defect.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis showing that the singular contribution to QFI with respect to tuning parameter m obeys universal power-law scaling, with renormalization-group arguments at the linearized fixed point to demonstrate protection from various factors like spatial dimensionality, anisotropies, and additional gapped bands.
AI.result: Established universal scaling law: QFI ∼ |m|^{p-2} for p ≠ 2, with logarithmic divergence ∼ ln(1/|m|) at p = 2, where p is the codimension of band-touching defects. This unifies SSH chains (p=1), Chern insulators (p=2), and Weyl semimetals (p=3) under a single codimension-dependent universality class, revealing only defects with p ≤ 2 generate divergent information-geometric responses.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a direct link between topological classification in momentum space and quantum distinguishability in parameter space, with implications for metrological sensitivity near topological transitions and experimental detection of topological criticality via quantum geometric observables.

title: DQC1-completeness of normalized trace estimation for functions of log-local Hamiltonians
summary:
We study the computational complexity of estimating the normalized trace $2^{-n}Tr[f(A)]$ for a log-local Hamiltonian $A$ acting on $n$ qubits. This problem arises naturally in the DQC1 model, yet its complexity is only understood for a limited class of functions $f(x)$.
  We show that if $f(x)$ is a continuous function with approximate degree $Ω({\rm poly}(n))$, then estimating $2^{-n}Tr[f(A)]$ up to constant additive error is DQC1-complete, under a technical condition on the polynomial approximation error of $f(x)$. This condition holds for a broad class of functions, including exponentials, trigonometric functions, logarithms, and inverse-type functions. We further prove that when $A$ is sparse, the classical query complexity of this problem is exponential in the approximate degree, assuming a conjectured lower bound for a trace variant of the $k$-Forrelation problem in the DQC1 query model. Together, these results identify the approximate degree as the key parameter governing the complexity of normalized trace estimation: it characterizes both the quantum complexity (via efficient DQC1 algorithms) and, conditionally, the classical hardness, yielding an exponential quantum-classical separation. Our proof develops a unified framework that cleanly combines circuit-to-Hamiltonian constructions, periodic Jacobi operators, and tools from polynomial approximation theory, including the Chebyshev equioscillation theorem.

AI.tldr: Normalized trace estimation for log-local Hamiltonians is DQC1-complete for functions with high approximate degree, revealing approximate degree as the key complexity parameter governing quantum-classical separation.
AI.motivation: The problem arises naturally in the DQC1 model of quantum computation, but its computational complexity is only understood for a limited class of functions. Understanding the complexity of estimating normalized traces of functions applied to Hamiltonians is fundamental for characterizing the power of quantum computation models.
AI.method: The paper develops a unified framework combining circuit-to-Hamiltonian constructions, periodic Jacobi operators, and polynomial approximation theory tools including the Chebyshev equioscillation theorem. It establishes DQC1-completeness for functions with Ω(poly(n)) approximate degree under technical conditions on polynomial approximation error.
AI.result: For continuous functions with high approximate degree, normalized trace estimation is DQC1-complete. For sparse Hamiltonians, classical query complexity is exponential in the approximate degree under a conjectured lower bound. Approximate degree emerges as the key parameter governing both quantum complexity (via efficient DQC1 algorithms) and classical hardness.
AI.conclusion: The approximate degree of functions is identified as the fundamental parameter determining the complexity of normalized trace estimation, characterizing both quantum efficiency and classical hardness, and yielding exponential quantum-classical separation for functions with high approximate degree.

title: Scalable Ground-State Certification of Quantum Spin Systems via Structured Noncommutative Polynomial Optimization
summary: A fundamental challenge in quantum physics is determining the ground-state properties of many-body systems. Whereas standard approaches, such as variational calculations, consist of writing down a wave function ansatz and minimizing over the possible states expressible by this ansatz, one can alternatively formulate the problem as a noncommutative polynomial optimization problem. This optimization problem can then be addressed using a hierarchy of semidefinite programming relaxations. In contrast to variational calculations, the semidefinite program can provide lower bounds for ground state energies and upper and lower bounds on observable expectation values. However, this approach typically suffers from severe scalability issues, limiting its applicability to small-to-medium-scale systems. In this article, we demonstrate that leveraging the inherent structures of the system can significantly mitigate these scalability challenges and thus allows us to compute meaningful bounds for quantum spin systems on up to $16\times16$ square lattices.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a scalable approach for computing rigorous bounds on ground-state properties of quantum many-body systems using semidefinite programming relaxations by exploiting system structure.
AI.motivation: Standard variational methods for determining ground-state properties of quantum many-body systems provide upper bounds but lack rigorous lower bounds. While semidefinite programming relaxations can provide both upper and lower bounds, they suffer from severe scalability issues that limit their applicability to small systems.
AI.method: The authors formulate the ground-state problem as a noncommutative polynomial optimization problem and address it using a hierarchy of semidefinite programming relaxations. The key innovation is leveraging the inherent structures of quantum spin systems to mitigate scalability challenges, enabling application to larger systems.
AI.result: The method successfully computes meaningful bounds for quantum spin systems on up to 16×16 square lattices, significantly extending the scale of systems that can be analyzed with rigorous bounds compared to previous approaches.
AI.conclusion: By exploiting system structure, semidefinite programming relaxations can be made scalable for computing rigorous bounds on ground-state properties of quantum many-body systems, overcoming previous limitations and enabling analysis of larger lattice systems.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Processing with Tensor-Network Frontends for Privacy-Aware Federated Medical Diagnosis
comment: Submitted to the IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering 2026
summary: We propose a privacy-aware hybrid framework for federated medical image classification that combines tensor-network representation learning, MPC-secured aggregation, and post-aggregation quantum refinement. The framework is motivated by two practical constraints in privacy-aware federated learning: MPC can introduce substantial communication overhead, and direct quantum processing of high-dimensional medical images is unrealistic with a small number of qubits. To address both constraints within a single architecture, client-side tensor-network frontends, Matrix Product State (MPS), Tree Tensor Network (TTN), and Multi-scale Entanglement Renormalization Ansatz (MERA), compress local inputs into compact latent representations, after which a Quantum-Enhanced Processor (QEP) refines the aggregated latent feature through quantum-state embedding and observable-based readout. Experiments on PneumoniaMNIST show that the effect of the QEP is frontend-dependent rather than uniform across architectures. In the present setting, the TTN+QEP combination exhibits the most balanced overall profile. The results also suggest that the QEP behaves more stably when the qubit count is sufficiently matched to the latent dimension, while noisy conditions degrade performance relative to the noiseless setting. The MPC benchmark further shows that communication cost is governed primarily by the dimension of the protected latent representation. This indicates that tensor-network compression plays a dual role: it enables small-qubit quantum processing on compressed latent features and reduces the communication overhead associated with secure aggregation. Taken together, these results support a co-design perspective in which representation compression, post-aggregation quantum refinement, and privacy-aware deployment should be optimized jointly.

AI.tldr: A privacy-aware hybrid federated learning framework for medical image classification combining tensor-network compression, MPC-secured aggregation, and post-aggregation quantum refinement to address communication overhead and quantum hardware limitations.
AI.motivation: Address two practical constraints in privacy-aware federated learning: 1) MPC introduces substantial communication overhead, and 2) direct quantum processing of high-dimensional medical images is unrealistic with limited qubits.
AI.method: Client-side tensor-network frontends (MPS, TTN, MERA) compress local medical images into compact latent representations. These are aggregated via MPC-secured aggregation, then refined by a Quantum-Enhanced Processor (QEP) using quantum-state embedding and observable-based readout.
AI.result: On PneumoniaMNIST, QEP effect is frontend-dependent (not uniform). TTN+QEP shows most balanced profile. QEP stability requires qubit count matching latent dimension. Noisy conditions degrade performance. MPC communication cost governed by latent dimension, showing tensor-network compression reduces both quantum processing requirements and communication overhead.
AI.conclusion: Tensor-network compression enables small-qubit quantum processing on compressed features while reducing secure aggregation communication overhead. Supports co-design perspective where representation compression, quantum refinement, and privacy-aware deployment should be jointly optimized.

title: Mechanism for scale-free skin effect in one-dimensional systems
summary: Non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE) is one of the most fascinating phenomena in non-Hermitian systems, which refers to enormous eigenstates localize at the boundary exponentially under open boundary condition (OBC). For typical NHSE, the localization length for a skin mode is independent of the system's size. Recently, some studies have revealed that for specific $1$-dimensional model, the localization length for eigenstates are proportional to the system's length under generalized boundary condition (GBC), and such phenomenon is dubbed as scale-free skin effect (SFSE). Further, SFSE is discovered in $1$-dimensional Hermitian chain with pure imaginary impurity at the end. In this work, we propose a mechanism for SFSE in 1-dimensional systems, which is model-independent. Our work provide a viewpoint for researching SFSE and shed new light on understanding finite size effect in non-Hermitian systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a model-independent mechanism for scale-free skin effect (SFSE) in 1D systems, where localization length scales with system size, unlike typical non-Hermitian skin effect.
AI.motivation: Recent discoveries show that in specific 1D models, localization length for eigenstates scales with system size under generalized boundary conditions (scale-free skin effect), which also appears in Hermitian chains with imaginary end impurities. The authors aim to develop a general, model-independent understanding of this phenomenon.
AI.method: The authors propose a mechanism for SFSE that is model-independent, providing a general framework applicable to various 1D systems rather than analyzing specific models.
AI.result: The work establishes a general mechanism explaining SFSE in 1D systems, offering insights into how localization length becomes proportional to system size under generalized boundary conditions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed model-independent mechanism provides a new perspective for researching SFSE and offers fresh understanding of finite size effects in non-Hermitian systems.

title: A Differentiable Physical Framework for Goal-Driven Spin-State Engineering in Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy
summary: Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (MRS) offers a unique non-invasive window into metabolic processes, yet its potential remains strictly constrained by severe spectral congestion and intrinsic insensitivity. Traditional pulse sequence design, tethered to human intuition, predominantly targets simple quantum states, thereby overlooking the vast majority of the exponentially scaling operator space which consists of complex spin superpositions. Here, we introduce a spectrum-driven, end-to-end differentiable physical framework that transcends these heuristic limitations. By integrating physical laws with automatic differentiation algorithm, our approach directly navigates the high-dimensional spin dynamics space, bypassing the intractable inverse problem of state preparation. This enables the discovery of non-intuitive, complex mixed states that simultaneously satisfy the dual objectives of selective excitation and interferometric signal enhancement. We validate this paradigm by achieving the robust separation of Glutamate and Glutamine, which is a longstanding neuroimaging challenge, in the human brain at 3T, demonstrating spectral fidelity superior to conventional methods. By unlocking the "dark" informational content of nuclear spin ensembles, our work establishes a generalizable paradigm for goal-driven quantum state engineering in magnetic resonance and beyond.

AI.tldr: A differentiable physical framework using automatic differentiation to design complex quantum states for MRS, enabling robust separation of Glutamate and Glutamine at 3T.
AI.motivation: MRS is limited by spectral congestion and low sensitivity. Traditional pulse sequence design, relying on human intuition, only targets simple quantum states, missing the vast majority of complex spin superpositions in the exponentially scaling operator space.
AI.method: A spectrum-driven, end-to-end differentiable physical framework that integrates physical laws with automatic differentiation to directly navigate high-dimensional spin dynamics space, bypassing the intractable inverse problem of state preparation.
AI.result: Achieved robust separation of Glutamate and Glutamine, a longstanding neuroimaging challenge, in the human brain at 3T, demonstrating spectral fidelity superior to conventional methods.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a generalizable paradigm for goal-driven quantum state engineering in magnetic resonance by unlocking the "dark" informational content of nuclear spin ensembles.

title: Distribution of Bell State Entanglement in Qubit Networks via Collision Models
summary: We propose a general scheme to controllably distribute pairwise entanglement in a quantum network of qubits by exploiting environmental ancilla qubits interacting with the network nodes through tunable Hamiltonians. Our approach leverages collision models, in which a quantum syatem interacts sequentially with ancilla units. We explore two distinct scenarios within this framework: one in which the ancilla is reset to its initial coherent state after each interaction (the traditional collision model), and another where the ancilla is not reset but its state is simply carried over to the next interaction, which we dub the repeated interaction model. In both scenarios, we ensure that the system-ancilla correlations are discarded between steps. We also demonstrate how varying the ancilla-system interaction patterns enables selective generation of entanglement between different qubit pairs, including non-neighbouring nodes that do not directly interact. The scheme is analyzed in networks up to three qubits under both collision and repeated interaction dynamics, revealing the genaration of maximally entangled bell pairs even in configurations where the interacting ancilla couples to only a single node. Our results provide a systematic and physically implementable route to entanglement distribution, offering potential applications in quantum communication, metrology and modular quantum computing.

AI.tldr: A scheme for distributing pairwise entanglement in quantum networks using environmental ancilla qubits and tunable Hamiltonians, analyzed through collision and repeated interaction models.
AI.motivation: To develop a systematic and physically implementable method for controllable entanglement distribution in quantum networks, addressing the challenge of generating entanglement between nodes that may not directly interact.
AI.method: Leverages collision models where network qubits interact sequentially with ancilla qubits through tunable Hamiltonians. Explores two scenarios: traditional collision model (ancilla reset after each interaction) and repeated interaction model (ancilla state carried over). System-ancilla correlations are discarded between steps, and varying interaction patterns enables selective entanglement generation.
AI.result: Demonstrates generation of maximally entangled Bell pairs in networks up to three qubits under both collision and repeated interaction dynamics. Shows entanglement can be generated even when ancilla couples to only a single node, and enables selective entanglement between different qubit pairs including non-neighboring nodes.
AI.conclusion: Provides a systematic and physically implementable route to entanglement distribution with potential applications in quantum communication, metrology, and modular quantum computing.

title: Topology-Hiding Path Validation for Large-Scale Quantum Key Distribution Networks
summary: Secure long-distance communication in quantum key distribution (QKD) networks depends on trusted repeater nodes along the entire transmission path. Consequently, these nodes will be subject to strict auditing and certification in future large-scale QKD deployments. However, trust must also extend to the network operator, who is responsible for fulfilling contractual obligations -- such as ensuring certified devices are used and transmission paths remain disjoint where required. In this work, we present a path validation protocol specifically designed for QKD networks. It enables the receiver to verify compliance with agreed-upon policies. At the same time, the protocol preserves the operator's confidentiality by ensuring that no sensitive information about the network topology is revealed to users. We provide a formal model and a provably secure generic construction of the protocol, along with a concrete instantiation. For long-distance communication involving 100 nodes, the protocol has a computational cost of 1-2.5s depending on the machine, and a communication overhead of less than 70kB - demonstrating the efficiency of our approach.

AI.tldr: A path validation protocol for QKD networks that allows receivers to verify policy compliance while preserving network topology confidentiality, with efficient performance for large networks.
AI.motivation: In QKD networks, trusted repeater nodes require auditing/certification, but trust must also extend to network operators who must ensure compliance with contractual obligations (certified devices, disjoint paths). Current approaches lack mechanisms for receivers to verify policy compliance without revealing sensitive network topology information.
AI.method: Developed a formal model and provably secure generic construction of a path validation protocol specifically designed for QKD networks. The protocol enables receivers to verify compliance with agreed-upon policies while preserving operator confidentiality by preventing disclosure of sensitive network topology information. Includes a concrete instantiation of the protocol.
AI.result: The protocol demonstrates practical efficiency: for long-distance communication involving 100 nodes, computational cost is 1-2.5 seconds (depending on machine) and communication overhead is less than 70kB. The protocol successfully achieves both policy verification and topology confidentiality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed path validation protocol provides an efficient solution for verifying policy compliance in QKD networks while maintaining operator confidentiality, addressing critical trust requirements for future large-scale QKD deployments.

title: Curvature-induced bound states in quantum wires
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, submitted to Phys. Rev. Research
summary: A classical particle under spatial constraints is strictly confined to live on a specific space manifold or path, but this assumption is incompatible with the zero-point fluctuations of a quantum particle. One way to describe quantum mechanics under constraints is the confinement potential approach (CPA). For a non-relativistic particle, the CPA maps the problem onto the solution of a Schrödinger-type equation in an isometrically embedded Riemannian submanifold of Euclidean space while the motion along orthogonal directions are decoupled and spatially confined. This approach respects quantum uncertainty, and one of its key results is the appearance of geometry- and metric-induced potentials that affect the stationary states and the dynamics of the particle. For particles constrained to different spaces, such as structures hosting sharp bents, vertices, wedges, conical apices, tips, or self-intersections, a formalism beyond the CPA is needed. Here, a step towards a CPA extension for irregular spaces is presented. After classifying the possible geometric irregularities concerning the CPA formalism, the presentation is focused on a sharply bent quantum wire modeled as an embedded curve with singular (but absolute integrable) curvature. For a subclass fulfilling the additional requirement that the geometric potential is a distribution of first order, a solution scheme for the confined Schrödinger equation is presented based on singular Sturm-Liouville theory and operator theoretic methods. The analytical considerations and numerical simulations evidence the existence of curvature-induced bound states with non-differentiable wave functions localized around the singular point, with an extension well beyond the singularity. Furthermore, a multitude of scattering states appear that may affect the transport and optical properties of the system.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an extension of the confinement potential approach (CPA) for quantum particles constrained to irregular spaces with geometric singularities, focusing on sharply bent quantum wires with singular curvature and developing analytical/numerical solutions showing curvature-induced bound states and scattering effects.
AI.motivation: Classical spatial constraints are incompatible with quantum zero-point fluctuations. While CPA handles quantum mechanics on smooth manifolds, it fails for irregular spaces with geometric singularities (sharp bends, vertices, wedges, conical apices, tips, self-intersections). A formalism beyond standard CPA is needed for such systems.
AI.method: 1) Classify geometric irregularities concerning CPA formalism. 2) Focus on sharply bent quantum wire modeled as embedded curve with singular (but absolutely integrable) curvature. 3) For subclass where geometric potential is first-order distribution, develop solution scheme using singular Sturm-Liouville theory and operator theoretic methods. 4) Combine analytical considerations with numerical simulations.
AI.result: Existence of curvature-induced bound states with non-differentiable wave functions localized around singular points, extending well beyond the singularity. Emergence of multitude of scattering states that may affect transport and optical properties. Analytical and numerical evidence supports these findings.
AI.conclusion: The work presents a step toward extending CPA to irregular spaces with geometric singularities, demonstrating that singular curvature can induce bound states with non-differentiable wave functions and scattering states with potential impact on quantum transport and optical properties in constrained systems.

title: Transversal non-Clifford gates on almost-good quantum LDPC and quantum locally testable codes
summary: We exhibit nontrivial transversal logical multi-controlled-$Z$ gates on $[\![N,Θ(N),\tildeΘ(N)]\!]$ quantum low-density parity-check codes and $[\![N,Θ(N),\tildeΘ(N)]\!]$ quantum locally testable codes with soundness $\tildeΘ(1)$, combining nearly optimal code parameters with fault-tolerant non-Clifford gates for the first time. Remarkably, our proofs are almost entirely algebraic-topological, showing that such presumably intricate logical gates naturally arise as a fundamental topological phenomenon. We develop a general framework for constructing a rich new family of homological invariant forms which we call ''cupcap gates'' that induce transversal logical multi-controlled-$Z$ and, building on insights from [Li et al., arXiv:2603.25831], covering space methods to certify their nontriviality. The claimed almost-good code results follow immediately as examples.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates nontrivial transversal logical multi-controlled-Z gates on nearly optimal quantum LDPC and locally testable codes, combining good code parameters with fault-tolerant non-Clifford gates for the first time using algebraic-topological methods.
AI.motivation: To achieve fault-tolerant quantum computation with non-Clifford gates on codes with near-optimal parameters, addressing the challenge of implementing logical non-Clifford operations while maintaining good code properties like distance and rate.
AI.method: Develops an algebraic-topological framework constructing "cupcap gates" as homological invariant forms that induce transversal logical multi-controlled-Z gates, using covering space methods to certify their nontriviality.
AI.result: Demonstrates nontrivial transversal logical multi-controlled-Z gates on quantum LDPC codes [N,Θ(N),Θ̃(N)] and quantum locally testable codes [N,Θ(N),Θ̃(N)] with soundness Θ̃(1), achieving nearly optimal code parameters with fault-tolerant non-Clifford gates.
AI.conclusion: The work shows that intricate logical gates naturally arise as fundamental topological phenomena, providing a new algebraic-topological approach to constructing fault-tolerant non-Clifford operations on high-performance quantum codes.

title: Phase-enhanced nonreciprocal photon-phonon conversion via coupled optomechanical cavities
summary: Nonreciprocity, characterized by direction-dependent signal propagation, is fundamental to technologies such as isolators, signal routing, and precision sensing. This letter theoretically demonstrates nonreciprocal phonon transport and the conversion between photon and acoustic phonon signals in coupled optomechanical cavities via phase-dependent driving. It is demonstrated that, in contrast to nonreciprocal phonon transport, which necessitates both dissipation and phase-induced violation of time reversal symmetry, the nonreciprocity in photon-phonon conversion can occur without violating time reversal symmetry. We demonstrate that such nonreciprocity arises due to the path-dependent asymmetry in photon-phonon conversion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the nonreciprocity of photon-phonon conversion can be further enhanced, achieving isolation levels of up to 40 dB by suitably modifying the phase difference of the driving lasers.

AI.tldr: Nonreciprocal phonon transport and photon-phonon conversion in optomechanical cavities via phase-dependent driving, with photon-phonon conversion achieving nonreciprocity without violating time reversal symmetry.
AI.motivation: Nonreciprocity enables crucial technologies like isolators and signal routing; this work explores nonreciprocal phenomena in optomechanical systems for enhanced signal control and conversion.
AI.method: Theoretical demonstration using coupled optomechanical cavities with phase-dependent driving, analyzing nonreciprocal phonon transport and photon-phonon conversion mechanisms.
AI.result: Photon-phonon conversion achieves nonreciprocity without violating time reversal symmetry due to path-dependent asymmetry, with isolation levels up to 40 dB achievable through optimized phase differences.
AI.conclusion: Phase-dependent driving enables distinct nonreciprocal mechanisms in optomechanical systems, with photon-phonon conversion offering unique nonreciprocity without time reversal symmetry violation, promising enhanced signal isolation capabilities.

title: A Loop-Shaping Approach to Coherent Feedback Control in Cavity Optomechanical Cooling
summary: We present a loop-shaping approach to coherent feedback (CF) control. By formulating the coupling between a quantum system and its environment in terms of the noise power spectrum, our method enables direct manipulation of the effective dissipation coefficients through spectral shaping. A systematic design framework for CF controllers is also developed, in which transfer functions are shaped to realize desired spectral responses.
