Applying this framework to optomechanical sideband cooling, we demonstrate that suppression of the Stokes process and enhancement of the anti-Stokes process can be simultaneously achieved, enabling ground-state cooling even in the unresolved-sideband regime. This loop-shaping framework provides an intuitive and general foundation for the design of CF controllers and can be extended to a wide class of quantum systems in which interactions with environments are characterized by noise power spectra.

AI.tldr: Loop-shaping approach to coherent feedback control enables manipulation of effective dissipation coefficients via spectral shaping, demonstrated for optomechanical sideband cooling.
AI.motivation: To develop a systematic design framework for coherent feedback controllers that can intuitively manipulate quantum system-environment interactions through spectral shaping.
AI.method: Formulate system-environment coupling via noise power spectrum; develop loop-shaping framework for CF controllers where transfer functions are shaped to achieve desired spectral responses.
AI.result: Demonstrated simultaneous suppression of Stokes process and enhancement of anti-Stokes process in optomechanical sideband cooling, enabling ground-state cooling even in unresolved-sideband regime.
AI.conclusion: The loop-shaping framework provides intuitive and general foundation for CF controller design, extendable to quantum systems where environment interactions are characterized by noise power spectra.

title: Universal critical timescales in slow non-Hermitian dynamics
summary: Non-Hermitian systems driven along slow parametric loops undergo non-adiabatic transitions whose outcome depends sensitively on the driving speed, yet no explicit formula has been available for the critical timescale $T_{\mathrm{cr}}$ at which these transitions develop. Using a $2\times 2$ Hamiltonian with circular parameter trajectories, we derive $T_{\mathrm{cr}} = \mathcal{G}\,\ln(1/|Δ|)$ in closed form for non-encircling loops, phase-shifted loops, offset loops, and loops encircling exceptional points, where $\mathcal{G}$ is a geometry-dependent growth factor and $Δ$ is the instability seed. This formula sharply separates the regime where the system remains in the averagely dominant eigenstate ($T< T_{\mathrm{cr}}$) from the superadiabatic regime where the instantaneous dominant eigenstate takes over ($T> T_{\mathrm{cr}}$), resolving the apparent tension between the previous literature. We identify two competing seeds: a geometric Stokes multiplier and the finite-precision floor. When the geometric seed vanishes, precision alone governs the transition, yielding $T_{\mathrm{cr}} \propto m\lnβ$, linear in the number of precision bits $m$. This provides a purely forward-evolution manifestation of precision-induced irreversibility (PIR)~\cite{PIR}, demonstrating that the fundamental limit identified through echo protocols also controls the outcome of slow non-Hermitian dynamics without requiring time reversal. For PT-symmetric energy spectra, $T_{\mathrm{cr}}$ additionally determines the onset of chirality: the dynamics is non-chiral for $T< T_{\mathrm{cr}}$ and chiral for $T> T_{\mathrm{cr}}$.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a closed-form formula for the critical timescale T_cr in non-Hermitian systems undergoing slow parametric driving, separating regimes where the system remains in the averagely dominant eigenstate from superadiabatic regimes where the instantaneous dominant eigenstate takes over.
AI.motivation: Non-Hermitian systems driven along slow parametric loops exhibit non-adiabatic transitions that depend sensitively on driving speed, but no explicit formula has been available for the critical timescale T_cr at which these transitions develop, creating apparent tension in previous literature.
AI.method: Using a 2×2 Hamiltonian with circular parameter trajectories, the authors derive T_cr = G ln(1/|Δ|) in closed form for various loop types (non-encircling, phase-shifted, offset, and loops encircling exceptional points), where G is a geometry-dependent growth factor and Δ is the instability seed.
AI.result: The formula sharply separates two regimes: T < T_cr where the system remains in the averagely dominant eigenstate, and T > T_cr where the instantaneous dominant eigenstate takes over (superadiabatic regime). When the geometric seed vanishes, precision alone governs the transition, yielding T_cr ∝ m lnβ, linear in the number of precision bits m, demonstrating precision-induced irreversibility (PIR) in forward evolution. For PT-symmetric energy spectra, T_cr determines the onset of chirality.
AI.conclusion: The derived formula resolves apparent tension in previous literature by providing an explicit critical timescale for non-adiabatic transitions in non-Hermitian systems. It reveals that the fundamental limit identified through echo protocols (PIR) also controls slow non-Hermitian dynamics without requiring time reversal, and establishes T_cr as the threshold for chirality onset in PT-symmetric systems.

title: Quantum-Inspired Geometric Classification with Correlation Group Structures and VQC Decision Modeling
summary: We propose a geometry-driven quantum-inspired classification framework that integrates Correlation Group Structures (CGR), compact SWAP-test-based overlap estimation, and selective variational quantum decision modelling. Rather than directly approximating class posteriors, the method adopts a geometry-first paradigm in which samples are evaluated relative to class medoids using overlap-derived Euclidean-like and angular similarity channels. CGR organizes features into anchor-centered correlation neighbourhoods, generating nonlinear, correlation-weighted representations that enhance robustness in heterogeneous tabular spaces. These geometric signals are fused through a non-probabilistic margin-based fusion score, serving as a lightweight and data-efficient primary classifier for small-to-moderate datasets. On Heart Disease, Breast Cancer, and Wine Quality datasets, the fusion-score classifier achieves 0.8478, 0.8881, and 0.9556 test accuracy respectively, with macro-F1 scores of 0.8463, 0.8703, and 0.9522, demonstrating competitive and stable performance relative to classical baselines. For large-scale and highly imbalanced regimes, we construct compact Delta-distance contrastive features and train a variational quantum classifier (VQC) as a nonlinear refinement layer. On the Credit Card Fraud dataset (0.17% prevalence), the Delta + VQC pipeline achieves approximately 0.85 minority recall at an alert rate of approximately 1.31%, with ROC-AUC 0.9249 and PR-AUC 0.3251 under full-dataset evaluation. These results highlight the importance of operating-point-aware assessment in rare-event detection and demonstrate that the proposed hybrid geometric-variational framework provides interpretable, scalable, and regime-adaptive classification across heterogeneous data settings.

AI.tldr: A hybrid quantum-inspired classification framework combining geometric correlation structures with variational quantum models for adaptive performance across different data regimes.
AI.motivation: To develop a classification framework that integrates geometry-driven quantum-inspired approaches for robust performance across heterogeneous tabular data, small-to-moderate datasets, and large-scale imbalanced regimes, while providing interpretable and scalable solutions.
AI.method: 1. Geometry-first paradigm using Correlation Group Structures (CGR) to organize features into anchor-centered correlation neighborhoods. 2. Compact SWAP-test-based overlap estimation for Euclidean-like and angular similarity channels. 3. Non-probabilistic margin-based fusion score as primary classifier. 4. For large imbalanced data: Delta-distance contrastive features + variational quantum classifier (VQC) as refinement layer.
AI.result: On standard datasets: Heart Disease (0.8478 accuracy, 0.8463 F1), Breast Cancer (0.8881 accuracy, 0.8703 F1), Wine Quality (0.9556 accuracy, 0.9522 F1). On Credit Card Fraud (0.17% prevalence): ~0.85 minority recall at ~1.31% alert rate, ROC-AUC 0.9249, PR-AUC 0.3251.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid geometric-variational framework provides interpretable, scalable, and regime-adaptive classification across heterogeneous data settings, highlighting the importance of operating-point-aware assessment in rare-event detection.

title: Towards Chemically Accurate and Scalable Quantum Simulations on IQM Quantum Hardware: A Quantum-HPC Hybrid Approach
summary: We present a large-scale experimental study of quantum-computing-based molecular simulation carried out on IQM's Sirius 24-qubit superconducting processor, utilizing up to 16 operational qubits. The work employs Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) together with the Local Unitary Cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) ansatz to estimate ground-state energies for a set of benchmark molecules, including H$_2$, LiH, BeH$_2$, H$_2$O, and NH$_3$. In addition, we introduce a Linear-CNOT variant of the Unitary Coupled-Cluster Singles and Doubles (LCNot-UCCSD) ansatz within the SQD workflow, trading higher circuit depth for reduced classical preprocessing. A comparison between these ansätze is provided, clarifying their respective strengths, limitations, and suitability for near-term quantum hardware. We further explore potential energy landscapes through 1D scans for H$_2$ and HeH$^+$ using both STO-3G and 6-31G basis sets, and for LiH and BeH$_2$ in STO-3G. Extending beyond this, we demonstrate the experimental construction of a full 2D potential energy surface for the water molecule on quantum hardware, mapped over a 32 $\times$ 32 grid in bond length and bond angle. To move beyond small benchmark systems, we combine SQD(LUCJ) with Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET) to compute active-space energies for a set of ligand-like molecules, as well as the pharmacologically relevant amantadine system. Across all studies, the majority of quantum-computed energies agree with reference FCI results, as well as with DMET-CASCI energies for embedded systems, to within chemical accuracy for the chosen basis sets. These results demonstrate the reliability of sample-based diagonalization approaches and underscore the potential of hybrid embedding strategies for extending quantum simulations to increasingly complex molecular systems, while also highlighting their practicality on current IQM quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: Experimental study of quantum molecular simulation on IQM's 24-qubit processor using Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization with LUCJ and LCNot-UCCSD ansätze, achieving chemical accuracy for benchmark molecules and demonstrating 2D potential energy surface construction and DMET embedding for larger systems.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate the practical application of quantum computing for molecular simulation on current near-term quantum hardware, specifically IQM's 24-qubit superconducting processor, and to explore the capabilities of sample-based diagonalization approaches combined with various ansätze for accurate ground-state energy estimation.
AI.method: Uses Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) with Local Unitary Cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) ansatz and introduces Linear-CNOT variant of Unitary Coupled-Cluster Singles and Doubles (LCNot-UCCSD) ansatz. Experiments conducted on IQM's Sirius 24-qubit superconducting processor with up to 16 operational qubits. Combines SQD(LUCJ) with Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET) for larger systems. Performs 1D potential energy scans and constructs 2D potential energy surfaces.
AI.result: Achieved chemical accuracy for ground-state energies of benchmark molecules (H₂, LiH, BeH₂, H₂O, NH₃) compared to reference FCI results. Successfully constructed full 2D potential energy surface for water molecule on quantum hardware over 32×32 grid. Demonstrated DMET-SQD(LUCJ) for ligand-like molecules and amantadine system, matching DMET-CASCI energies. Majority of quantum-computed energies agreed with reference results within chemical accuracy for chosen basis sets.
AI.conclusion: Sample-based diagonalization approaches are reliable for quantum molecular simulation on current hardware. Hybrid embedding strategies (DMET-SQD) extend quantum simulations to complex molecular systems. The work demonstrates practicality of quantum computing for chemical applications on near-term quantum hardware while highlighting trade-offs between different ansätze for circuit depth and classical preprocessing requirements.

title: Compact system development of efficient quantum-entangled photon sources towards deployable and industrial devices
summary: Entangled photon pair sources are a key enabling technology for quantum communication and networking, yet their deployment beyond laboratory environments is hindered by system-level complexity, limited operational stability, and insufficient industry compatibility. Here, we demonstrate a rack-based, mobile quantum light source architecture based on a semiconductor quantum dot emitter that directly addresses these challenges through modular system integration and automated operation. The source generates polarization-entangled photon pairs with an entanglement negativity 2n of up to $0.98(1)$, confirming near-maximal entanglement quality. In continuous, hands-off operation over a six-hour time window, the system achieves an average single-photon emission rate of $697(8)$ kHz and a maximum rate of $740(7)$ kHz, while maintaining 2n-value of more than $95$ $\%$. These results are enabled by the integration of optical excitation, collection, cryogenic operation, and control electronics within a standardized rack footprint, together with automated monitoring. By demonstrating simultaneously high entanglement quality, sustained brightness, and long-term operational stability in an industry-aligned system architecture, this work advances semiconductor quantum dot sources toward deployable entangled photon sources for applied quantum photonics.

AI.tldr: A rack-based, mobile quantum light source using semiconductor quantum dots achieves high entanglement quality (negativity up to 0.98), sustained brightness (~700 kHz), and long-term stability in industry-compatible architecture.
AI.motivation: Current entangled photon pair sources face deployment challenges due to system complexity, limited operational stability, and insufficient industry compatibility, hindering their use beyond laboratory environments.
AI.method: Developed a rack-based, mobile quantum light source architecture using semiconductor quantum dot emitter with modular system integration and automated operation. Integrated optical excitation, collection, cryogenic operation, and control electronics within standardized rack footprint with automated monitoring.
AI.result: Achieved polarization-entangled photon pairs with entanglement negativity up to 0.98(1), confirming near-maximal entanglement quality. In continuous six-hour operation: average single-photon emission rate of 697(8) kHz, maximum rate of 740(7) kHz, while maintaining >95% of maximum negativity value.
AI.conclusion: The work advances semiconductor quantum dot sources toward deployable entangled photon sources for applied quantum photonics by demonstrating simultaneously high entanglement quality, sustained brightness, and long-term operational stability in an industry-aligned system architecture.

title: Perspectives in and on Quantum Theory
summary: I take a pragmatist perspective on quantum theory. This is not a view of the world described by quantum theory. In this view quantum theory itself does not describe the physical world, nor our observatons, experiences or opinions of it. Instead, the theory offers reliable advice on when to expect an event of one kind or another, and on how strongly to expect each possible outcome of that event. The actual outcome is a perspectival fact: a fact relative to a physical context of assessment. Measurement outcomes and quantum states are both perspectival. By noticing that each must be relativized to an appropriate physical context one can resolve the measurement problem and the problem of nonlocal action. But if the outcome of a quantum measurement is not an absolute fact, then why shoud the statistics of such outcomes give us any objective reason to accept quantum theory? One can describe extensions of the scenario of Wigner's friend in which a statement expressing the outcome of a quantum measurement would be true relative to one such context but not relative to another. However, physical conditions in our world prevent us from realizing such scenarios. Since the outcome of every actual quantum measurement is certified at what is essentially a single context of assessment, the outcome relative to that context is an objective fact in the only sense that matters for science. We should accept quantum theory because the statistics these outcomes display are just those it leads us to expect.

AI.tldr: A pragmatist interpretation of quantum theory where quantum states and measurement outcomes are perspectival facts relative to physical contexts, resolving measurement and nonlocality problems while maintaining scientific objectivity.
AI.motivation: To address foundational problems in quantum mechanics (measurement problem and nonlocality) by developing a pragmatist interpretation that treats quantum theory as providing reliable advice about expectations rather than describing reality directly.
AI.method: Adopts a pragmatist philosophical perspective where quantum theory offers predictive advice about event probabilities. Treats measurement outcomes and quantum states as perspectival facts relativized to physical contexts of assessment. Analyzes Wigner's friend scenarios to illustrate context relativity while arguing that physical constraints in our world prevent problematic contradictions.
AI.result: Resolves measurement problem and nonlocality issues by relativizing outcomes to contexts. Shows that while outcomes are perspectival, actual measurements occur in single contexts making them objective for scientific purposes. Demonstrates that quantum statistics remain reliable despite perspectival nature of individual outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Quantum theory should be accepted because it provides accurate statistical predictions. The perspectival nature of outcomes doesn't undermine scientific objectivity since actual measurements are certified in single contexts, making their statistics objectively reliable for scientific purposes.

title: Quantum search algorithm for similar subgraph identification under fixed edge removal
summary: We introduce a novel quantum algorithm for similar subgraph identification in form of an NP-hard cardinality-constrained binary quadratic optimization problem. Given a weighted reference graph with Laplacian $\boldsymbol{B}$, our algorithm determines the subgraph featuring Laplacian $\boldsymbol{B'}$ on the same vertex set, but $x$ out of $N$ inactive edges, minimizing the Frobenius distance $||\boldsymbol{B} - \boldsymbol{B'}||_\mathrm{F}^2$. We represent the $\binom{N}{x}$ graph topologies by an equal-weight superposition in form of a Dicke state, enabling controlled transformations applied to the quantum state associated with the vectorized Laplacian of the reference graph. Combined with amplitude estimation and a minimum finding approach, our algorithm provides a polynomial speed up $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N^{x}/x!}N\log\log N)$ compared to $\mathcal{O}(N^{x+1}/x!)$ of classical brute-force search algorithms. We demonstrate the application of our method on standard test cases, which represent electric power grids, by reconstructing $||\boldsymbol{B} -\boldsymbol{B'}||_\mathrm{F}^2$ from measurements and show how our approach can be additionally used to calculate energy functional like quadratic forms of the Laplacians with respect to a given vector.

AI.tldr: Quantum algorithm for similar subgraph identification using Dicke states and amplitude estimation achieves polynomial speedup over classical brute-force search for NP-hard graph optimization problem.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the NP-hard problem of identifying similar subgraphs in weighted graphs, which has applications in areas like electric power grid analysis. Classical brute-force approaches have exponential complexity, motivating the development of quantum algorithms for polynomial speedup.
AI.method: The method encodes all possible graph topologies (with x inactive edges out of N) as an equal-weight superposition using Dicke states. Controlled transformations are applied to the quantum state representing the vectorized Laplacian of the reference graph. The algorithm combines amplitude estimation with minimum finding to identify the subgraph minimizing the Frobenius distance between Laplacians.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves a polynomial speedup of O(√(N^x/x!)N log log N) compared to classical brute-force complexity O(N^{x+1}/x!). The method is demonstrated on standard test cases representing electric power grids, successfully reconstructing Frobenius distances from measurements and calculating energy functionals like quadratic forms of Laplacians.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum algorithm provides an efficient solution for similar subgraph identification with provable polynomial speedup over classical approaches, demonstrating practical applications in network analysis and energy functional calculations.

authors: Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente
title: High-threshold decoding of non-Pauli codes for 2D universality
summary: Topological codes have many desirable properties that allow fault-tolerant quantum computation with relatively low overhead. A core challenge for these codes, however, is to achieve a low-overhead universal gate set with limited connectivity. In this work, we explore a non-Pauli stabilizer code that can be used to complete a universal gate set on topological toric and surface codes in strictly two dimensions. Fault-tolerant syndrome extraction for the non-Pauli code requires mid-circuit $X$ corrections, a key difference to conventional Pauli codes. We construct and benchmark a just-in-time (JIT) matching decoder to reliably decide these corrections. Under a phenomenological error model with equally likely physical and measurement errors, we find a high threshold of $\approx 2.5\,\%$, close to the $\approx 2.9\,\%$ of a decoder with access to the full syndrome history. We also perform a finite-size scaling analysis to estimate how the logical error rate scales below threshold and verify an exponential suppression in both physical error rate and in the system size. A second global decoding step for $Z$ errors is required and the non-Clifford gates in the circuit reduce the threshold from $\approx 2.9\,\%$ to $\approx 1.8\,\%$ with a naive decoder. We show how $Z$ decoding can be improved using knowledge of the $X$ corrections, pushing the threshold to $\approx 2.2\,\%$. Our results suggest non-Clifford logic in 2D codes could perform comparably to 2D quantum memory. Our formalism for efficient benchmarking and decoding directly generalizes to a broader family of CSS codes whose $X$ stabilizers are twisted by diagonal Clifford operators, and spacetime versions thereof, defined by CSS-like circuits enriched by $CCZ$, $CS$, and $T$ gates.

AI.tldr: A non-Pauli stabilizer code enables universal gate sets on 2D topological codes, requiring mid-circuit X corrections and a novel JIT matching decoder, achieving thresholds up to 2.5%.
AI.motivation: Topological codes need low-overhead universal gate sets with limited connectivity in 2D architectures. Conventional Pauli codes face challenges in achieving fault-tolerant non-Clifford operations.
AI.method: Develop a non-Pauli stabilizer code for toric/surface codes, implement just-in-time matching decoder for mid-circuit X corrections, perform phenomenological error modeling, and conduct finite-size scaling analysis.
AI.result: Achieved threshold of ≈2.5% with JIT decoder (close to 2.9% full-history decoder), exponential suppression of logical errors, improved Z decoding to 2.2% threshold from 1.8% naive decoder.
AI.conclusion: Non-Clifford logic in 2D codes can perform comparably to 2D quantum memory, with formalism generalizable to CSS codes twisted by diagonal Clifford operators and spacetime versions with CCZ, CS, and T gates.

title: Quantitative Universal Approximation for Noisy Quantum Neural Networks
summary: We provide here a universal approximation theorem with precise quantitative error bounds for noisy quantum neural networks. We focus on applications to Quantitative Finance, where target functions are often given as expectations. We further provide a detailed numerical analysis, testing our results on actual noisy quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: Universal approximation theorem with quantitative error bounds for noisy quantum neural networks, applied to Quantitative Finance with expectations as target functions, validated on actual noisy quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: To establish rigorous theoretical foundations for quantum neural networks operating in realistic noisy environments, particularly for financial applications where functions are often expressed as expectations, and to bridge the gap between theory and practical implementation on current quantum hardware.
AI.method: Develops a universal approximation theorem with precise quantitative error bounds specifically for noisy quantum neural networks, applies this framework to Quantitative Finance problems where target functions are expectations, and conducts detailed numerical analysis including validation on actual noisy quantum hardware.
AI.result: Provides theoretical guarantees for noisy quantum neural networks' approximation capabilities with explicit error bounds, demonstrates applicability to financial problems, and shows practical feasibility through successful testing on real quantum hardware despite noise.
AI.conclusion: Noisy quantum neural networks can effectively approximate financial expectation functions with quantifiable error bounds, and the theoretical framework is validated by practical implementation on current noisy quantum hardware, advancing both quantum machine learning theory and financial applications.

title: Photonic qubit encoding interconversion for heterogeneous quantum networking
summary: Quantum information processing, communication, and sensing networks are being developed with various qubit platforms that use different encoding schemes. Connecting quantum network nodes to distribute entanglement requires matching photon qubit basis encoding. In this work, we implement an interconversion protocol which converts photon qubit encoding from the polarization basis to the time-bin basis, transmits the photons through a transport fiber with large fluctuations in polarization, and converts back to polarization encoding for ease of measurement. This interconversion scheme faithfully transmits a polarization Bell state across the transport fiber by converting sources of infidelity to changes in transmission rate. These results illustrate a practical approach for interfacing distinct qubit platforms to enable modular and flexible operation in heterogeneous quantum networks.

AI.tldr: Interconversion protocol converts photon qubit encoding between polarization and time-bin bases to enable entanglement distribution across heterogeneous quantum networks with polarization-stable transmission.
AI.motivation: Quantum networks use diverse qubit platforms with different encoding schemes, requiring matching photon qubit basis encoding for entanglement distribution. Polarization encoding suffers from fluctuations in transport fibers, necessitating a conversion scheme to enable modular operation across heterogeneous platforms.
AI.method: Implemented an interconversion protocol that converts photon qubit encoding from polarization basis to time-bin basis, transmits through transport fiber with polarization fluctuations, then converts back to polarization encoding for measurement. This scheme converts sources of infidelity to changes in transmission rate rather than quantum state corruption.
AI.result: Successfully transmitted a polarization Bell state across transport fiber with large polarization fluctuations by using the interconversion scheme. The protocol faithfully preserves quantum information by converting infidelity sources to transmission rate variations rather than state corruption.
AI.conclusion: The interconversion approach provides a practical method for interfacing distinct qubit platforms, enabling modular and flexible operation in heterogeneous quantum networks by overcoming polarization instability in transport fibers through basis conversion.

title: Constrained Quantum Optimization via Iterative Warm-Start XY-Mixers
summary: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a leading hybrid heuristic for combinatorial optimization, but efficiently handling hard constraints remains a significant challenge. XY-mixers successfully confine quantum state evolution to a feasible subspace, such as the Hamming-weight-1 sector for one-hot constraints. On the contrary, warm-starting biases the search toward promising regions based on preliminary solutions. Combining these two techniques requires maintaining the essential alignment between the initial state and the mixer Hamiltonian to preserve convergence guarantees. Previous work demonstrated warm-starting with XY-mixers via a biased initial state, but relying only on standard mixer Hamiltonians. Consequently, the initial state is no longer a ground state of the mixer. In this work, we overcome these limitations by formulating a warm-started XY-mixer Hamiltonian for one-hot constraints and proving its ground-state properties. Furthermore, we provide a shallow circuit implementation suitable for NISQ implementations. We embed the warm-starting into a classical heuristic that iteratively updates the bias based on previous samples, called Iterative Warm-Starting (IWS). Extensive numerical simulations on Max-$k$-Cut and Traveling Salesperson Problem instances demonstrate that IWS-QAOA significantly accelerates the solution-finding process, increasing the probability of sampling optimal solutions by orders of magnitude compared to standard XY-QAOA. Finally, we validate our approach on the ibm_boston QPU using hardware-tailored 144-qubit problem instances. By coupling IWS-QAOA with a greedy steepest-descent post-processing strategy to repair infeasible measurements caused by hardware noise, we successfully identify optimal solutions on actual quantum devices.

AI.tldr: IWS-QAOA combines warm-starting with XY-mixers for constrained optimization, using iterative bias updates and hardware-tailored implementation to significantly improve solution quality on quantum devices.
AI.motivation: QAOA struggles with hard constraints in combinatorial optimization. While XY-mixers confine evolution to feasible subspaces and warm-starting biases toward promising regions, combining them properly while maintaining convergence guarantees remains challenging due to misalignment between initial states and mixer Hamiltonians.
AI.method: Developed warm-started XY-mixer Hamiltonian for one-hot constraints with proven ground-state properties. Created shallow circuit implementation for NISQ devices. Embedded warm-starting into Iterative Warm-Starting (IWS) heuristic that updates bias based on previous samples. Combined with greedy steepest-descent post-processing to repair infeasible measurements from hardware noise.
AI.result: IWS-QAOA significantly accelerates solution-finding, increasing optimal solution probability by orders of magnitude vs standard XY-QAOA on Max-k-Cut and TSP instances. Validated on ibm_boston QPU with 144-qubit hardware-tailored instances, successfully identifying optimal solutions on actual quantum devices when combined with noise repair strategy.
AI.conclusion: The work successfully integrates warm-starting with XY-mixers for constrained optimization, providing theoretical guarantees, practical implementation, and experimental validation on quantum hardware, demonstrating substantial performance improvements for combinatorial optimization problems.

title: Q2NS Demo: A Quantum Network Simulator Based on ns-3
comment: This work has been funded by the European Union under Horizon Europe ERC-CoG grant QNattyNet, n.101169850. Views and opinions expressed are however those of the author(s) only and do not necessarily reflect those of the European Union or the European Research Council Executive Agency. summary: Q2NS is an open-source quantum network simulator built on ns-3, the de facto standard for classical network simulation. By inheriting ns-3's mature classical stack and event-driven execution model, Q2NS enables faithful co-simulation of quantum-network dynamics and classical signaling, a core requirement for the functioning of any quantum network. Its modular architecture is designed for extensibility, with pluggable quantum-state backends (state-vector, density matrix, stabilizer) and a clean separation between network control and node-level operations. Q2NS comes with a quantum network visualizer Q2NSViz, supporting interactive inspection of both physical- and entanglement-induced connectivity graphs, helping users interpret protocol behavior and entanglement manipulation processes. We present a demonstration of Q2NS, highlighting its ability to capture and simulate the coexistence of quantum and classical communication. The proposed demonstration presents quantum communication scenarios of increasing complexity: from entanglement distribution basics to multipartite graph-state manipulation, complemented by pre-loaded examples in Q2NSViz that require no prior quantum communication or coding experience.

AI.tldr: Q2NS is an open-source quantum network simulator built on ns-3 that enables co-simulation of quantum and classical network dynamics with modular architecture and visualization tools.
AI.motivation: There is a need for simulation tools that can faithfully model the coexistence and interaction of quantum and classical communication in quantum networks, which is essential for protocol development and testing.
AI.method: Built on ns-3's mature classical stack and event-driven execution model, Q2NS uses modular architecture with pluggable quantum-state backends (state-vector, density matrix, stabilizer) and clean separation between network control and node-level operations.
AI.result: Q2NS successfully enables co-simulation of quantum-network dynamics and classical signaling, comes with Q2NSViz visualizer for interactive inspection of connectivity graphs, and demonstrates ability to simulate quantum communication scenarios from basic entanglement distribution to multipartite graph-state manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Q2NS provides a comprehensive, extensible simulation platform for quantum networks that bridges quantum and classical communication, with visualization tools that make quantum network concepts accessible to users without prior quantum communication experience.

title: The Phase Quantum Walk: A Unified Framework for Graph State Distribution in Quantum Networks
summary: Distributing arbitrary graph states across quantum networks is a central challenge for modular quantum computing and measurement-based quantum communication. I introduce the phase quantum walk (PQW), a discrete-time quantum walk in which the conventional position-permuting shift operator is replaced by a diagonal conditional phase (CZ) gate, enabling distribution of arbitrary graph states, not merely GHZ states, from elementary two-qubit resources. The Byproduct Lemma shows that each walk step teleports edge entanglement with a correctable Pauli byproduct; the Coin Invariance Theorem proves that the optimal fidelity F*(C,E) = F*(H,E) for all unitary coins C and noise channels E, with closed-form expressions F_dep = (1 - 3p/4)^k and F_pd = ((1 + sqrt(1 - p))/2)^k. Analytical correction formulas are derived for tree graphs (general theorem) and ring graphs (C4 case study), with F = 1.0 verified across eight topologies (up to 4096 outcomes). Hardware validation on ibm marrakesh (IBM Heron r2, CZ-native) yields F_cl = 0.924 for |GHZ4> and 0.922 for |L4>, statistically identical, providing the first experimental confirmation that fidelity is independent of graph topology as predicted by the Coin Invariance Theorem.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Phase Quantum Walk (PQW) for distributing arbitrary graph states across quantum networks, proving fidelity is independent of graph topology via Coin Invariance Theorem and demonstrating experimental validation on IBM hardware.
AI.motivation: Distributing arbitrary graph states (beyond just GHZ states) across quantum networks is essential for modular quantum computing and measurement-based quantum communication, but existing methods are limited.
AI.method: Introduces Phase Quantum Walk (PQW) which replaces conventional shift operators with diagonal conditional phase (CZ) gates, enabling distribution from elementary two-qubit resources. Includes Byproduct Lemma for teleportation with correctable Pauli byproducts and Coin Invariance Theorem for fidelity analysis.
AI.result: Derived closed-form fidelity expressions: F_dep = (1 - 3p/4)^k and F_pd = ((1 + sqrt(1 - p))/2)^k. Analytical correction formulas for tree and ring graphs. Experimental validation on IBM Heron r2 (ibm_marrakesh) shows F_cl = 0.924 for |GHZ4> and 0.922 for |L4>, confirming fidelity independence from graph topology.
AI.conclusion: PQW enables distribution of arbitrary graph states (not just GHZ states) with topology-independent fidelity, experimentally validated on quantum hardware, advancing modular quantum computing and measurement-based quantum communication.

title: Shot-to-shot noise cancellation for parametric oscillators
summary: Powerful approaches to squeeze the motional state of a harmonic oscillator rely on the stepwise modulation of its resonance frequency. Such protocols can be limited by forces that vary slowly between experimental runs but are constant during a single experimental shot. Such shot-to-shot noise gives rise to a spread in experimental outcomes that masks the uncertainty intrinsic to quantum theory. Taking inspiration from spin-echo protocols, we propose a decoupling technique that, under ideal conditions, perfectly cancels shot-to-shot force noise in squeezing experiments based on parametric modulation. We implement the protocol using an optically levitated nanoparticle, where shot-to-shot force noise arises from slowly varying stray fields acting on the charge carried by the particle. Using our oscillator-echo protocol, we demonstrate shot-to-shot noise suppression to the measurement-backaction limit.

AI.tldr: Researchers developed an "oscillator-echo" protocol inspired by spin-echo techniques to cancel shot-to-shot force noise in parametric squeezing experiments with optically levitated nanoparticles, achieving noise suppression to the measurement-backaction limit.
AI.motivation: Parametric squeezing protocols for harmonic oscillators are limited by shot-to-shot force noise - slowly varying forces between experimental runs that mask intrinsic quantum uncertainty. This noise arises from stray fields acting on charged particles in levitated nanoparticle systems.
AI.method: Developed a decoupling technique inspired by spin-echo protocols that perfectly cancels shot-to-shot force noise under ideal conditions. Implemented using an optically levitated nanoparticle where force noise comes from slowly varying stray fields acting on particle charge.
AI.result: Successfully demonstrated shot-to-shot noise suppression to the measurement-backaction limit using the oscillator-echo protocol with optically levitated nanoparticles.
AI.conclusion: The oscillator-echo protocol effectively cancels shot-to-shot force noise in parametric squeezing experiments, enabling observation of intrinsic quantum uncertainty by suppressing technical noise to fundamental measurement-backaction limits.

title: A Pragmatist Understanding of Quantum Mechanics
summary: Applications of quantum mechanics have led to many successful predictions and explanations of puzzling phenomena, and we now apply quantum mechanics to gain, process, and communicate information in novel ways. We can understand quantum mechanics by understanding how we have applied it. We should not seek agreement on the nature of the world it represents, because this theory does not itself represent the physical world (though its applications do help us to represent it better). When applied to a quantum state, quantum mechanics yields probabiities for physical events: both state and probability are objective--not because they represent elements of phyiscal reality, but because each exerts norrmative authority over the beliefs of anyone who accepts quantum mechanics and applies it relative to a physical situation they may (but need not) occupy. These events may be described by statements that are meaningful in an appropriate environmental context, and quantum mechanics can help one to say when that is. Measurement creates an appropriate context, so here the Born rule indirectly yields probabilities of measurement outcomes. The quantum state of a system does not "collapse" on measurement: a new state must be assigned relative to a physical situation in which information about the outcome is accessible. Understood this way, there is no measurement problem, and violations of Bell inequalities does not demonstrate "spooky" non-local action. Quantum field theories have no physical ontology of their own: a quantum field is a mathematical object in a model whose application helps us to improve and extend our descriptions of the world in other terms. We cannot realise the scenario of Wigner's friend and its recent extensions: but the data that provide overwhelming evidence for quantum mechanics are objective in the same sense as the relative measurement outcomes described in those scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that quantum mechanics should be understood as a normative framework for belief formation rather than a direct representation of physical reality, resolving measurement problems and non-locality issues through a contextual, information-based interpretation.
AI.motivation: To address persistent interpretational problems in quantum mechanics (measurement problem, wavefunction collapse, non-locality) by proposing that quantum theory doesn't directly represent physical reality but provides normative rules for forming beliefs about physical situations.
AI.method: Develops a philosophical interpretation where quantum states and probabilities are objective normative entities rather than representations of physical reality, emphasizing contextual application, information accessibility, and the Born rule as providing belief constraints rather than physical descriptions.
AI.result: Resolves measurement problem without collapse, explains Bell inequality violations without non-local action, interprets quantum fields as mathematical tools rather than physical entities, and shows Wigner's friend scenarios as unrealizable while maintaining objectivity of quantum evidence.
AI.conclusion: Quantum mechanics should be understood as providing objective normative constraints on beliefs about physical situations rather than representing physical reality directly, eliminating traditional interpretational problems while preserving the theory's empirical success.

title: High-bandwidth Coherence Cloning using Optical-Phase-Locking Feedforward
summary: Ultra-narrow-linewidth lasers with suppressed high-frequency phase noise are critical for quantum control and precision metrology. While optical phase locking (OPL) is the standard technique for cloning the coherence of such sources, its effectiveness is often limited at high frequencies by feedback latency. We present a robust feedforward architecture that overcomes this limitation by recycling and demodulating the existing master-slave beat signal to drive a single electro-optic modulator for near-instantaneous noise cancellation. This approach eliminates the extraneous sidebands and transmission losses typical of more complex modulators. Through active stabilization of the beat amplitude and demodulation phase, we demonstrate robust suppression exceeding 30 dB from 10 kHz to 10 MHz. This hardware-efficient framework is readily compatible with standard OPL setups, offering a scalable solution for high-fidelity coherent control.

AI.tldr: Feedforward architecture for ultra-narrow-linewidth lasers overcomes OPL latency limitations by recycling beat signal for near-instantaneous noise cancellation, achieving >30 dB suppression from 10 kHz to 10 MHz.
AI.motivation: Optical phase locking (OPL) is limited at high frequencies by feedback latency, restricting its effectiveness for quantum control and precision metrology applications requiring ultra-narrow-linewidth lasers with suppressed high-frequency phase noise.
AI.method: Robust feedforward architecture that recycles and demodulates existing master-slave beat signal to drive a single electro-optic modulator for near-instantaneous noise cancellation, eliminating extraneous sidebands and transmission losses typical of complex modulators. Active stabilization of beat amplitude and demodulation phase ensures robust performance.
AI.result: Demonstrated robust suppression exceeding 30 dB from 10 kHz to 10 MHz, overcoming OPL latency limitations with hardware-efficient framework compatible with standard OPL setups.
AI.conclusion: The feedforward approach offers a scalable solution for high-fidelity coherent control by providing near-instantaneous noise cancellation without the latency limitations of traditional OPL, enabling improved performance for quantum control and precision metrology applications.

title: Quantum Time-Space Tradeoffs for Exponential Dynamic Programming
summary: We investigate the quantum algorithms for dynamic programming by Ambainis et al. (SODA'19). While giving provable complexity speedups and applicable to a variety of NP-hard problems, these algorithms have a notable drawback: they require a large amount of Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM), which potentially could be very challenging to implement in a physical quantum computer. In this work, we study how we can improve the space complexity by trading it for time, while still retaining a speedup over the classical algorithms. We show novel quantum time-space tradeoffs, which we obtain by adjusting the parameters of these algorithms and combining them with "quantized" classical strategies.

AI.tldr: Quantum time-space tradeoffs for dynamic programming algorithms by adjusting parameters and combining with classical strategies to reduce QRAM requirements while maintaining speedups.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum dynamic programming algorithms by Ambainis et al. provide provable speedups for NP-hard problems but require large amounts of QRAM, which is challenging to implement physically. The authors aim to improve space complexity by trading it for time while retaining quantum speedups over classical algorithms.
AI.method: Adjust parameters of existing quantum dynamic programming algorithms and combine them with "quantized" classical strategies to achieve time-space tradeoffs.
AI.result: Novel quantum time-space tradeoffs that reduce QRAM requirements while maintaining computational speedups over classical algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that quantum dynamic programming algorithms can be made more practical by trading space for time, achieving a balance between resource requirements and computational advantages.

title: Explicit constructions of mutually unbiased bases via Hadamard matrices
summary: We present a detailed computational and algebraic study of Mutually Unbiased Bases (MUBs) in finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, with a particular focus on dimensions 2, 3, 4, and the challenging case of 6. Starting from the Hadamard-phase parametrization, we derive explicit analytical conditions for mutual unbiasedness in dimension 4, providing a tractable system of trigonometric constraints on the phase parameters. We then explore a tensor-product construction via Pauli operators, highlighting the algebraic and group-theoretical origin of MUBs in two-qubit systems, and demonstrating how these constructions yield a complete set of 5 MUBs in dimension 4. Extending our approach, we investigate the Fourier-family method in dimension 6, where the absence of a prime-power structure imposes strong rigidity constraints and limits the known constructions to sets of 3 MUBs. We provide a systematic computational framework for testing candidate phase vectors, bridging the gap between analytical insight and numerical exploration. Finally, we generalize the discussion to arbitrary prime-power dimensions, emphasizing the role of finite-field structures, Heisenberg-Weyl operators, and discrete symmetries in generating complete sets of MUBs. Our work offers a transparent, line-by-line verification methodology, highlighting both the geometric and algebraic richness of MUBs, and clarifying why certain dimensions resist full analytical constructions. This study serves as a comprehensive resource for researchers seeking both theoretical understanding and practical construction of MUBs in quantum information science.

AI.tldr: Analytical and computational study of Mutually Unbiased Bases (MUBs) in finite dimensions, focusing on explicit constructions in dimensions 2,3,4,6 and general prime-power dimensions, with emphasis on algebraic structures and verification methods.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive computational and algebraic framework for understanding and constructing Mutually Unbiased Bases (MUBs) across various finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, particularly addressing the challenging case of dimension 6 and clarifying why certain dimensions resist complete constructions.
AI.method: 1. Hadamard-phase parametrization for deriving explicit analytical conditions in dimension 4; 2. Tensor-product construction via Pauli operators for two-qubit systems; 3. Fourier-family method for dimension 6; 4. Systematic computational framework for testing candidate phase vectors; 5. Generalization to prime-power dimensions using finite-field structures, Heisenberg-Weyl operators, and discrete symmetries.
AI.result: 1. Derived explicit trigonometric constraints for MUBs in dimension 4; 2. Demonstrated complete set of 5 MUBs in dimension 4 via Pauli operator construction; 3. Showed limitation to 3 MUBs in dimension 6 due to non-prime-power structure; 4. Developed transparent verification methodology bridging analytical insight and numerical exploration; 5. Established connection between MUB constructions and finite-field algebraic structures.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a comprehensive resource for MUB construction in quantum information science, highlighting the geometric and algebraic richness of MUBs while clarifying why certain dimensions (like 6) resist full analytical constructions due to their non-prime-power structure and associated rigidity constraints.

title: Lemniscate phase trajectories for high-fidelity GHZ state preparation in trapped-ion chains
summary: In trapped-ion chains, multipartite GHZ states can be prepared natively with the help of a single bichromatic laser pulse. However, higher-order terms in the expansion in the Lamb-Dicke parameter $η$ limit the GHZ state preparation infidelity for rectangular and bell-like pulses to the order of $η^4$. For tens of ions, the infidelity caused by out-of-Lamb-Dicke effects can reach several percents. We propose an amplitude and phase-modulated pulse shape, an "echoed lemniscate pulse", which cancels this contribution into error in the leading order. For the proposed pulse, the infidelity scales as $η^6$. The improved scaling is achieved because of a special phase trajectory of a collective motional mode following the figure-eight curve (lemniscate). We demonstrate that the lemniscate pulse allows achieving lower infidelity than bell-like pulses, which can be as low as $10^{-4}$ for $20$-ion chains.

AI.tldr: Proposed an amplitude and phase-modulated "echoed lemniscate pulse" for trapped-ion GHZ state preparation that cancels leading-order Lamb-Dicke errors, achieving η⁶ infidelity scaling vs η⁴ for conventional pulses.
AI.motivation: Multipartite GHZ state preparation in trapped-ion chains using bichromatic laser pulses suffers from infidelity limitations due to higher-order Lamb-Dicke parameter terms, reaching several percent for tens of ions with conventional rectangular and bell-like pulses.
AI.method: Developed an amplitude and phase-modulated pulse shape called "echoed lemniscate pulse" that creates a special phase trajectory where the collective motional mode follows a figure-eight curve (lemniscate), enabling cancellation of leading-order Lamb-Dicke errors.
AI.result: The lemniscate pulse achieves infidelity scaling as η⁶ compared to η⁴ for conventional pulses, enabling infidelities as low as 10⁻⁴ for 20-ion chains, significantly outperforming bell-like pulses.
AI.conclusion: The echoed lemniscate pulse provides superior GHZ state preparation fidelity in trapped-ion systems by canceling leading-order Lamb-Dicke errors through engineered phase trajectories, enabling high-fidelity multipartite entanglement for quantum information processing.

title: Space-Efficient Quantum Algorithm for Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithms with Resource Estimation
summary: Solving the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP) is critical for evaluating the quantum security of widely deployed elliptic-curve cryptosystems. Consequently, minimizing the number of logical qubits required to execute this algorithm is a key object. In implementations of Shor's algorithm, the space complexity is largely dictated by the modular inversion operation during point addition. Starting from the extended Euclidean algorithm (EEA), we refine the register-sharing method of Proos and Zalka and propose a space-efficient reversible modular inversion algorithm. We use length registers together with location-controlled arithmetic to store the intermediate variables in a compact form throughout the computation. We then optimize the stepwise update rules and give concrete circuit constructions for the resulting controlled arithmetic components. This leads to a modular inversion circuit that uses $3n + 4\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + O(1)$ logical qubits and $204n^2\log_2 n + O(n^2)$ Toffoli gates. By inserting this modular inversion component into the controlled affine point-addition circuit, we obtain a space-efficient algorithm for the ECDLP with $5n + 4\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + O(1)$ qubits and $O(n^3)$ Toffoli gates. In particular, for a 256-bit prime-field curve, our estimate reduces the logical-qubit count to 1333, compared with 2124 in the previous low-width implementation of Häner et al.

AI.tldr: Space-efficient quantum algorithm for elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem using optimized modular inversion circuit with reduced qubit count.
AI.motivation: Minimizing logical qubit requirements for Shor's algorithm on elliptic curve cryptography is crucial for evaluating quantum security and practical implementation feasibility.
AI.method: Refined register-sharing method from extended Euclidean algorithm, using length registers with location-controlled arithmetic for compact variable storage, optimized stepwise update rules, and concrete circuit constructions for controlled arithmetic components.
AI.result: Achieved modular inversion circuit with 3n + 4⌊log₂n⌋ + O(1) qubits and 204n²log₂n + O(n²) Toffoli gates; ECDLP algorithm with 5n + 4⌊log₂n⌋ + O(1) qubits and O(n³) Toffoli gates; reduced 256-bit implementation from 2124 to 1333 logical qubits.
AI.conclusion: Significant space reduction for quantum ECDLP attacks enables more practical quantum cryptanalysis of elliptic curve systems with current quantum computing constraints.

title: Towards High-Brightness Perfect Photon Blockade
summary: Single-photon sources with high single-photon purity and high brightness are key elements of many future quantum technologies. While photon blockade (PB) is widely exploited in the development of such sources, achieving the coexistence of high purity and high brightness remains a long-standing challenge. Here, we identify a novel mechanism for high-brightness PB and demonstrate that near-ideal purity and near-ideal brightness can be simultaneously achieved in an extended nondegenerate two-photon Jaynes-Cummings model with two-body and three-body interactions. This mechanism is underpinned by a distinctive energy-level structure arising from the combined action of the two interactions. The energy levels in the multi-excitation manifold essentially retain a harmonic ladder of degenerate doublets, whereas in the single-excitation subspace the doublet degeneracy is lifted, with a finite splitting between the two levels. Consequently, when one bosonic mode is driven by a coherent continuous-wave pump, the former degeneracy enables the other bosonic mode to exhibit near-perfect PB even in the strong driving regime, while the latter splitting allows the mean photon number of that mode to approach unity. Our proposed scheme overcomes the outstanding challenge and offers a promising pathway toward realizing ideal single-photon sources.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel photon blockade mechanism using an extended nondegenerate two-photon Jaynes-Cummings model with two-body and three-body interactions to achieve simultaneous near-ideal single-photon purity and brightness.
AI.motivation: Achieving both high single-photon purity and high brightness in single-photon sources remains a long-standing challenge despite widespread use of photon blockade mechanisms. Current approaches struggle to simultaneously optimize both metrics.
AI.method: The authors develop an extended nondegenerate two-photon Jaynes-Cummings model incorporating both two-body and three-body interactions. This creates a distinctive energy-level structure where multi-excitation manifolds maintain harmonic ladder degeneracy while single-excitation subspaces have lifted degeneracy with finite splitting.
AI.result: The proposed mechanism enables near-perfect photon blockade in the strong driving regime, with the mean photon number approaching unity. This simultaneously achieves near-ideal purity and near-ideal brightness, overcoming previous limitations.
AI.conclusion: The novel photon blockade mechanism offers a promising pathway toward realizing ideal single-photon sources by simultaneously achieving high purity and high brightness, addressing a fundamental challenge in quantum technology development.
